messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for chiming in.

I'd like to add that if you have:

  parameters {
    real<lower=0> phi;
  ...
  model {
    1 / phi ~ normal(0,1)

then the non-linear change of variables means you need to add the
Jacobian correction

  log | d/d.phi (1 / phi) |

to the log density if you want phi to have the right distribution:

  increment_log_prob(pow(phi,-2));

Beta binomial is built in as beta_binomial.

dirichlet_multinomial isn't built in yet, but we should definitely include
it.  I created the feature request:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1130

On the topic of multinomials, we also need to work on K-1 parameter versions
that implicitly apply the K-1 version of softmax (one input constrained to 0),
and there's already an issue for that:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/266

- Bob

We have to get more serious

> On Nov 11, 2014, at 5:12 AM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I fitted a negative binomial model last weekend, and noticed that prior for phi of neg_binomial_2 made a big difference. I didn't found a good prior for phi itself, but (half-)normal(0, s)  as a prior for 1/phi works well, at least when s=1. From mvcv I knew that phi would be around 4–10.
>
> Also tried individual-level normal and cauchy random effects, for the data has some large residuals, but these were too slow.
>
> (BTW, I wouldn't mind if Stan had beta-binomial and dirichlet-multinomial built in. I needed to code the latter manually yesterday. These distributions are a bit like negative binomial in the sense that they handle the overdispersion of count data, and are faster than leaving the intermediate individual-level "random effects" to be sampled.)
>
>
> On Tuesday, November 11, 2014 6:57:04 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But it's the sampling efficiency that's more worrying and also
> more difficult to diagnose.  We've started playing with some negative
> binomials to implement the Zheng et al. paper:
>

Thanks so much for the reply. That makes a lot of sense thinking about it as left censoring as opposed to just a truncated distribution. The example Stan lines are really helpful.

> you just need
>
>   increment_log_prob(N_censored_below * weibull_cdf_log(1, alpha, sigma));
>
> Note this uses the CDF, not the CCDF, because it's the total probability from
> 0 (the lower bound of support for Weibull) to 1.
>
> 2. Censoring above.
>
> For the species still alive, you need to know when they originated to know
> what the censoring point is --- if species n arose (no idea what the
> right term is here) at time t_origin[n] and is not yet
> extinct at t_current, then you know the survival time is somewhere
> above (t_current - t_origin[n]).  For each such observation, you censor with
> its own bounds.  In Stan:
>
>  for (n in 1:N_censored_above)
>    increment_log_prob(weibull_ccdf_log(t_current - t_origin[n], alpha, sigma);
>
> If t_origin is a vector of size N_truncated_above, you can vectorize to
> just
>
>  increment_log_prob(weibull_ccdf_log(t_current - t_origin, alpha, sigma);
>
> This uses the CCDF because it's 1 - CDF(U) to indicate the true value is
> somewhere above U.
>
> 3. Uncensored
>
> For species with survival time greater than 1 who are extinct, there's no
> truncation needed.  In Stan, in vector form, that's
>
>  dur_unc ~ weibull(alpha, sigma);
>
> 4.  Priors
>
> I have no idea what the scale of survival times is, but you want
> the priors to be consistent with the expected posteriors.  Especially
> when you don't have a lot of data.   There's a relevant section
> in the regression chapter of the current (v2.5) Stan language manual that discusses
> priors for scales --- the same arguments apply here.  Also, with gamma, you
> should double check the parameterization --- we use shape and inverse scale (aka rate).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Nov 10, 2014, at 4:17 PM, Peter Smits <thesti...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear List,
> >
> > Sorry if this is a bit of a beginner question. I'm mostly new to this level of modeling and Bayesian data analysis and don't come a statistics background at all.
> >
> > I'm wondering about how to update the log-probability of censored data from a truncated distribution.
> >
> > I'm writing a survival model of species fossil durations. Because the fossil record is resolvable only to a certain degree of accuracy, there is a minimum duration for all observed species. In this case, the minimum duration is 1. Also, because not all species are extinct a few of the observations are right censored.
> >
> > From the manual, I understand that for truncated distributions I first increment the log probability by the log of the sampling distribution and then subtract the log of the complementary cumulative density function evaluated at the truncation point from the log probability. I also know that for integrating over the censored observations, I increment the log probability by the log of the complementary cumulative density function. My concern is do I need to then subtract some value from the log probability? And if so, what?
> >
> > Following the suggestions from BDA, the STAN manual, and various posts on this list I've been able to write a model that I believe is at least heading in the right direction. Attached is a short Stan model that fits a Weibull distribution to the observed durations. I've implemented truncation for the uncensored observations, but I'm stuck on what to do with the censored observations. I've also attached an R object (as ASCII file using dput) of the data I'm using. Hopefully this works as a minimal example.

> > Thanks in advance for any advice. Again, I'm relatively new to this whole business.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving ODEs for time arrays of different sizes
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Solving ODEs for time arrays of different sizes
messages.body_plain:
Stan has arrays of vectors, but they all have to be the same size.
Adding ragged arrays is a fairly big project and one of the things on
our current round of grant proposals :-)  Along with sparse matrices.
And structured matrices.

For now, you need to use an indexing hack.  There are various examples
in the manual, but they need to be updated to use our slicing functions.
I should really add a whole chapter, so I added it to the next-manual to-do list:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-62575137

The short answer is to do something like this:

  int[N] size;
  real[K] values;

  int pos;
  pos <- 1;
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real[sizes[n]] value_n;
    values_n <- slice(values, pos, size[n]);

    ... do what you want with values_n ...

For instance, if you had the equivalent of R's list(c(10,9),c(8,7,6),c(5))
you would have

  size = { 2, 3, 1 }
  values = { 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 }

- Bob

P.S.  Given that we just rolled out the ODE solver, we'd be
      interested in getting feedback on how it works.  We're still encountering
      some issues with long integration times when the sampler gets into
      regions of the posterior that stiffen the ODE.  One of our highest-priority
      issues at the moment is dealing with this issue --- our plan is to plug in
      lsoda as the general integrator (workhorse of deSolve in R), but any advice
      on integrators, etc., is appreciated --- none of us are specialists in
      general numerical integration.

messages.subject: Re: pairs() in RStan?
messages.subject_clean: pairs() in RStan?
messages.body_plain:
Here's my modified pairs method that I use with Rstan fits. It doesn't plot in the lower diagonal, but rather just displays the correlation value.

It does however require extracting the samples first, e.g. post <- extract(fit), then you can pass whichever samples you like to the function. You could also do the conditions on the samples first, before passing them in.

You'll see in the code how each portion of the plot is defined separately. If you don't want anything in the lower diagonal, just set lower.panel=NULL in the last line of the function.

mcmcpairs <- function( posterior , n=500 , cex=0.7 , pch=16 , adj=1 , ...) {
    panel.dens <- function(x, ...) {
        usr <- par("usr"); on.exit(par(usr))
        par(usr = c(usr[1:2], 0, 1.5) )
        h <- density(x,adj=adj)
        y <- h$y
        y <- y/max(y)
        abline( v=0 , col="gray" , lwd=0.5 )
        lines( h$x , y )
    }
    panel.2d <- function( x , y , ... ) {
        i <- sample( 1:length(x) , size=n )
        abline( v=0 , col="gray" , lwd=0.5 )
        abline( h=0 , col="gray" , lwd=0.5 )
        dcols <- densCols( x[i] , y[i] )
        points( x[i] , y[i] , col=dcols , ... )
    }
    panel.cor <- function( x , y , ... ) {
        k <- cor( x , y )
        cx <- sum(range(x))/2
        cy <- sum(range(y))/2
        text( cx , cy , round(k,2) , cex=2*exp(abs(k))/exp(1) )
    }
    pairs( posterior , cex=cex , pch=pch , upper.panel=panel.2d , lower.panel=panel.cor , diag.panel=panel.dens , ... )
}

Thanks for your quick feedback Bob.

The problem is that I want to use "value_n" as time argument for the "integrate_ode" function which has to be in the "transformed parameters" or "model" block, which means that "value_n" won't be data any more but a parameter, which is not an option for the time argument (data only).

What you suggested is what I tried in the PK_ODE_02.stan (previous email). Any other work-around here?

Also, am I right that the time argument for "integrate_ode" can't be a single real value but has to be an array of real values? In other words, can I get the solution of the ODEs for just ONE time point?

BW
Thierry

Le mardi 11 novembre 2014 16:49:05 UTC, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> Stan has arrays of vectors, but they all have to be the same size.
> Adding ragged arrays is a fairly big project and one of the things on
> our current round of grant proposals :-)  Along with sparse matrices.
> And structured matrices.
>
> For now, you need to use an indexing hack.  There are various examples
> in the manual, but they need to be updated to use our slicing functions.
> I should really add a whole chapter, so I added it to the next-manual to-do list:
>
>   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-62575137
>
> The short answer is to do something like this:
>
>   int[N] size;
>   real[K] values;
>
>   int pos;
>   pos <- 1;
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     real[sizes[n]] value_n;
>     values_n <- slice(values, pos, size[n]);
>
>     ... do what you want with values_n ...
>
> For instance, if you had the equivalent of R's list(c(10,9),c(8,7,6),c(5))
> you would have
>
>   size = { 2, 3, 1 }
>   values = { 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 }
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Given that we just rolled out the ODE solver, we'd be
>       interested in getting feedback on how it works.  We're still encountering
>       some issues with long integration times when the sampler gets into
>       regions of the posterior that stiffen the ODE.  One of our highest-priority
>       issues at the moment is dealing with this issue --- our plan is to plug in
>       lsoda as the general integrator (workhorse of deSolve in R), but any advice
>       on integrators, etc., is appreciated --- none of us are specialists in
>       general numerical integration.
>

On 11/10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's a motivation I hadn't thought about.
>
> Restarting adaptation is a bit trickier because we're
> using online estimators for the mass matrix.  To properly
> restart from exactly where we left off, those would need
> to be dumped too, which is exposing a lot more of our internals
> to the outside than I'm comfortable with.  So maybe we could
> compromise and just store mass matrix and step size at some
> point and put a little more burden on the caller to rewind
> and restart from the last saved state.  But that could lose

Hi Thierry,

Thanks for trying it out.... unfortunately, it looks like a bug in the Stan compiler. I've got a reproducible model that touches the problem. It's issue #1131 in Stan. Hopefully we can get it fixed soon.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1131

Daniel

On Tue, Nov 11, 2014 at 10:04 AM, Thierry Wendling <thierry....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks for your quick feedback Bob.
>
> The problem is that I want to use "value_n" as time argument for the "integrate_ode" function which has to be in the "transformed parameters" or "model" block, which means that "value_n" won't be data any more but a parameter, which is not an option for the time argument (data only).
>
> What you suggested is what I tried in the PK_ODE_02.stan (previous email). Any other work-around here?
>
> Also, am I right that the time argument for "integrate_ode" can't be a single real value but has to be an array of real values? In other words, can I get the solution of the ODEs for just ONE time point?
>
> BW
> Thierry
>
> Le mardi 11 novembre 2014 16:49:05 UTC, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> > Stan has arrays of vectors, but they all have to be the same size.
> > Adding ragged arrays is a fairly big project and one of the things on
> > our current round of grant proposals :-)  Along with sparse matrices.
> > And structured matrices.
> >
> > For now, you need to use an indexing hack.  There are various examples
> > in the manual, but they need to be updated to use our slicing functions.
> > I should really add a whole chapter, so I added it to the next-manual to-do list:
> >
> >   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-62575137
> >
> > The short answer is to do something like this:
> >
> >   int[N] size;
> >   real[K] values;
> >
> >   int pos;
> >   pos <- 1;
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     real[sizes[n]] value_n;
> >     values_n <- slice(values, pos, size[n]);
> >
> >     ... do what you want with values_n ...
> >
> > For instance, if you had the equivalent of R's list(c(10,9),c(8,7,6),c(5))
> > you would have
> >
> >   size = { 2, 3, 1 }
> >   values = { 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 }
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > P.S.  Given that we just rolled out the ODE solver, we'd be
> >       interested in getting feedback on how it works.  We're still encountering
> >       some issues with long integration times when the sampler gets into
> >       regions of the posterior that stiffen the ODE.  One of our highest-priority
> >       issues at the moment is dealing with this issue --- our plan is to plug in
> >       lsoda as the general integrator (workhorse of deSolve in R), but any advice
> >       on integrators, etc., is appreciated --- none of us are specialists in
> >       general numerical integration.
> >
> > > On Nov 11, 2014, at 5:28 AM, Thierry Wendling <thierry....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear Stan team and users,
> > >
> > > I'm trying to analyse population pharmacokinetic data (drug concentration-time data for several individuals) using a mixed-effects model defined with two ODEs. Since the subjects in the dataset have time vectors of different lengths, I'm struggling to provide individual time vectors (all appended in one "TIME" vector) adequately for the "integrate_ode" function.
> > > I usually deal with this issue using a list of vectors in R or cells in MATLAB but I believe Stan doesn't support such data structures? I thus tried:
> > >         • to solve the equations for each time point for each subject, i.e. for each element of the "TIME" vector (see "transformed parameters" block in PK_ODE.stan), but the time argument in the "integrate_ode" function has to be an array of real numbers and can apparently not be a single real number:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >         • to provide the time vector for each individual using the "segment" function (see  "transformed parameters" block in PK_ODE_02.stan), but the time argument in the "integrate_ode" function has to be pure data:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Any suggestion to deal with this problem?
> > >
> > > Many thanks in advance for your help.
> > >
> > > BW,
> > > Thierry Wendling

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Resuming stoped chains
messages.body_plain:
Do you really need full Bayes for that?   Are you doing
downstream inference with the parameter estimation uncertainty?

If not, are the posterior means or medians that different
different than what you'd get with a penalized MLE?

This is exactly the kind of problem for which we want to expand
our MLE capabilities to use Laplace approximations of uncertainty.
Not to mention apply MML, VB, or EP for hierarchical models.  Sorry
we're not there yet!

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Resuming stoped chains
messages.body_plain:
Similar here, a large logistic regression. I agree with you, Bob, there is not need to really do full Bayes here. But it is just a prototype for a research paper - so some other motivations are behind this.

There is another point where resuming chains would be useful: Our cluster has multiple queues, and the "short" one has a super high throughput and many many cores available, so queuing time is less, etc. So if I can run my MCMC chains on there, there will be way less overhead. However, walltime limit is under an hour. Now I would like to run my stan jobs in that queue, restart them a few times to finish, and get *exactly* the same result as running the chain on one go. Just an engineering point mostly, and for reproducible experiments.

Am Mittwoch, 12. November 2014 06:47:04 UTC schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> Do you really need full Bayes for that?   Are you doing
> downstream inference with the parameter estimation uncertainty?
>
> If not, are the posterior means or medians that different
> different than what you'd get with a penalized MLE?
>
> This is exactly the kind of problem for which we want to expand
> our MLE capabilities to use Laplace approximations of uncertainty.
> Not to mention apply MML, VB, or EP for hierarchical models.  Sorry
> we're not there yet!
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 11, 2014, at 11:44 AM, Allen Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> >
> > On 11/10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> That's a motivation I hadn't thought about.
> >>
> >> Restarting adaptation is a bit trickier because we're
> >> using online estimators for the mass matrix.  To properly
> >> restart from exactly where we left off, those would need
> >> to be dumped too, which is exposing a lot more of our internals
> >> to the outside than I'm comfortable with.  So maybe we could
> >> compromise and just store mass matrix and step size at some
> >> point and put a little more burden on the caller to rewind
> >> and restart from the last saved state.  But that could lose
> >> days in a 6 day run.
> >>
> >> By the way, what's taking 6 days to run?
> >>
> >
> > Logistic regression with NxP = 80000 x 500
> >

Looking at the data I can see some large drops in weekly averages, and I estimate the weekly averages are affected about 70% of the time, to varying degrees.

messages.body_plain:
Sorry if this is obvious, maybe it isn't for all who want to do logistic regression with Stan:

If there's no hierarchy, that is if priors are fixed,  and priors are differentiable (not like Lasso/L1), one can take the MAP estimate with Stan's optimizing(). The default LBFGS is fine,  and let it compute the Hessian (I haven't tried that). Then 1.96*sqrt(diag(solve(-hessian))) gives you the 95% confidence intervals based on the first-order Laplace approximation. (Or is it called second order because the first derivative vanishes?)

If you are not using R, "solve" above is the inverse.

Joint MAP of all parameters is not so good for estimating hierarchies, or "automatic shrinkage". So there a strategy for large data is to use the Laplace approximation internally in the optimization algorithm, something the current Stan cannot do.

On Wednesday, November 12, 2014 5:39:28 PM UTC+2, Allen Riddell wrote:
> I see. Yes, Laplace approx would be fine in this case. It would be great if Stan
> could do that for us!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Solving ODEs for time arrays of different sizes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thierry,

There's a workaround that you can implement now. The idea is to take f_index and move it to the transformed data block as an array and compute the offsets.

Here's what it looks like:
transformed data {
 ...
  int f_index[Nsub];
  f_index[1] <-1;
  for (i in 2:Nsub) {
    f_index[i] <- f_index[i-1] + Nobs[i];
  }
}
...
transformed parameters {
  ...
  for (i in 1:Nsub) {
        real sol[Nobs[i],2];
         sol <- integrate_ode(IVinf_2cmt,
                         y0, t0, segment(TIME, f_index[i], Nobs[i]), theta[i],
                         DOSING[i], x_i);
  ...

I'm attaching the whole model that compiles. (I don't know if the model actually samples properly.) There was another bug in the code where one of the loops was incorrectly specified (can't remember where exactly.)

Can you let us know if this helps?

messages.subject: intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories
messages.subject_clean: intercept and efficiency in a multilevel logit model w/ categories
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have logit model with two categorical covariates (let's call them A
and B) and a bunch of continuous covariates C. In simple least squares, I
would just drop the first category for each categorical covariate,
define coefficients relative to that, and include an intercept.

However, I have good reasons to impose a multilevel distribution on
each group of coefficients, eg

a_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_a);
b_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
c_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_c);

(The full model is below). I have the following questions:

1. What are the best practices for coding this kind of model in Stan, in
terms of sampling efficiency? Currently, I am including an intercept (a
nuisance parameter) -- strictly speaking, the coefficients for A and B
are not identified per se, so I transform them relative to the first one
each. I found that this gives rather efficient samples, but I am
wondering what is recommended. Textbook discussions of similar models
that use Gibbs sampling consider various other techniques to enhance
convergence, but it looks like Stan works fine without them, relative
n_eff of the model below is about 30-90%.

messages.body_plain:
Responses inline.

> On Nov 13, 2014, at 8:53 AM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I have logit model with two categorical covariates (let's call them A
> and B) and a bunch of continuous covariates C. In simple least squares, I
> would just drop the first category for each categorical covariate,
> define coefficients relative to that, and include an intercept.
>
> However, I have good reasons to impose a multilevel distribution on
> each group of coefficients, eg
>
> a_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_a);
> b_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
> c_coeff ~ normal(0, sigma_c);
>
> (The full model is below). I have the following questions:
>
> 1. What are the best practices for coding this kind of model in Stan, in
> terms of sampling efficiency? Currently, I am including an intercept (a
> nuisance parameter) -- strictly speaking, the coefficients for A and B
> are not identified per se, so I transform them relative to the first one
> each. I found that this gives rather efficient samples, but I am
> wondering what is recommended. Textbook discussions of similar models
> that use Gibbs sampling consider various other techniques to enhance
> convergence, but it looks like Stan works fine without them, relative
> n_eff of the model below is about 30-90%.

This is tricky.  We've talked about this with Andrew with
no real clear advice on how to put priors on these things
so that the model's both identified and not overly constrained.

The problems it presents are outlined in the problematic posteriors
chapter of the Stan language manual.   The addition of a hierarchical
prior for the two coeffs may be solving your issue because you
center both around 0 and there are other terms in the equation
helping to control matters.

Gelman and Hill recommend normalizing this way for Gibbs
samplers, as you point out, but I'm not convinced it even makes sense
there given that you're still trying to sample from an improper posterior
(at least if you don't put priors on the coeffs).  Andrew assures
me it's OK, but doesn't think it's worth formalizing now that we're
not using Gibbs.

There's a new section in the 2.5 manual in the problematic
posteriors section called "mitigating the invariances", which
describes some strategies to remediate non-identifiability, which
you get with this part of your model:

 for (i in 1:N) {
    x[i] <- a_coeff[a[i]] + b_coeff[b[i]];
  }
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(intercept + x + c * c_coeff);

I'm surprised the model you attached worked so well in Stan.  Is
that the n_eff for parameters, or for the normalized coeffs?  If
everything declared as a parameter has decent convergence and lp__
also does, you should be OK.  There's also a new section in the manual
on convergence --- Michael's been setting me straight on the theory.

> 2. I avoid constructing the monster design matrix and use a loop instead
> for categorical covariates, then add the continuous covariates using a
> matrix product (see below), is this the recommended way?

Yes.  That's the most efficient way to write it.

>
> 3. Any other remarks would be appreciated -- this is a stylized version
> but the full model has more categorical covariates so I would rather try
> to work towards something that samples efficiently, even if that means
> more complicated code.

I'd highly recommend doing what you're doing --- starting simple and
working up!

I'm surprised this works well without a prior on intercept.  But it's
really all about how well the data constrain the posterior geometry.
You might also want to add priors for the sigma, but if you have
enough data that the posterior's well behaved, it's not necessary.
Stan technically only requires the posterior to be proper.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thierry,

I too have been struggling with the ODE solver in Stan 2.5. I found I need to carefully constrain the parameters to prevent combinations of value that result in stiff equations or near discontinuities. When I allowed parameters to be unconstrained or have large supports, Stan would often attempt some extreme parameter values. The result is that the solver would spin for hours without a result.

Bob et al: consider this a plea to implement a version of integrate_ode that provides arguments for setting error tolerances and limits on step size or number of steps--and that will exit with an error message when such limits are exceeded rather than apparently going into an infinite loop.

I have also dealt with the problem of analyzing popPK data from patients with different numbers of observations. The attached Stan code illustrates the approach I used. It implements a linear 2 compartment model with 1st order absorption--a testing exercise since it is solvable analytically. The data set is based on NONMEM conventions for representing dose events. The corresponding R code and data set is attached. This is simulated data I have used at Metrum for teaching an introductory Bayesian analysis course using WinBUGS.

Cheers,
Bill

Thanks for the examples.  None of the members of the Stan
dev team have much experience with numerical integrators,
so we really appreciate the feedback (including all the
great advice we've gotten already).

Bill --- your plea's already been anticipated. I
ran into the same problem a few days ago and filed a
feature request:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1127

Bill's diagnosis is correct --- you need to ensure the parameters
don't wander into stiff territory.

We are definitely going to

A.  include a variable stiffness solver like lsoda;  already
on our near term to-do list, and

B.  allow user control of absolute and relative tolerances.

See the discussion of the issue for reasons we don't just want
to throttle number of steps (short answer --- same reason we
don't want to limit number of leapfrog steps in the HMC integrator ---
we don't want to bias results).

For now, I found the following two steps should help:

1.  lowering initial step size to something like .01 or even
lower

2.  increasing accept target to 0.9 or even higher

In RStan, this will look like:

  fit <- stan("soil_incubation.stan",
              data=c("totalC_t0", "t0", "T", "ts", "eCO2"),
              control=list(adapt_delta=0.95,
                           stepsize=0.01),
              chains=4, iter=4000, seed=1234);

Without the control parameters, the integrator would just
grind to a halt.

(1) will force Stan to take small steps to start and (2) will
make sure the step size doesn't grow too much during adaptation (small
step sizes are needed to guarantee high acceptance rates).
Small step sizes allow Stan's HMC simulation to follow the curvature
of the posterior more closely and avoid low density areas that tend
to be stiff.

- Bob

On Thu, Nov 13 2014, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I'm surprised the model you attached worked so well in Stan.  Is
> that the n_eff for parameters, or for the normalized coeffs?  If
> everything declared as a parameter has decent convergence and lp__
> also does, you should be OK.  There's also a new section in the manual
> on convergence --- Michael's been setting me straight on the theory.

It turns out that the model can be improved, by putting a prior on the
sigma_'s (half-Cauchy) and the intercept (vague normal, see full model
below). For the original, Rhat for lp__ is about 1.1, now it is down to
1.01, the priors for the intercept and the sigmas contribute about half
the improvement, respectively. Statistics for 3 chains:

                      n_eff Rhat
intercept                83 1.04
a_coeff[1]               75 1.06
a_coeff[2]               72 1.06
a_coeff[3]               75 1.06
b_coeff[1]               81 1.04
b_coeff[2]               83 1.04
b_coeff[3]               93 1.03
c_coeff[1]              345 1.00
c_coeff[2]              280 1.00
sigma_a                 173 1.02
sigma_b                 186 1.00
sigma_c                 223 1.01
normalized_a_coeff[1]   750  NaN
normalized_a_coeff[2]   532 1.00
normalized_a_coeff[3]   422 1.00
normalized_b_coeff[1]   750  NaN
normalized_b_coeff[2]   383 1.00
normalized_b_coeff[3]   382 1.01
lp__                    185 1.01

The good n_eff, of course, is always for the normalized coefficients.

For the list archives, I saved this model at
https://gist.github.com/tpapp/c42f3f3a5f184fcd8403 . I know Cauchy is
excessive, and a uniform would be OK, too.

Thanks for the help!

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jasper,

I think the free AMI instances have too little RAM to compile a Stan model with g++. The first thing to do would be to install clang++ from a shell via

sudo apt-get install clang++

Then, again from a shell, you need to tell R to use clang rather than g++ by executing

mkdir -p ~/.R
echo "CC=clang" >> ~/.R/Makevars
echo "CXX=clang++" >> ~/.R/Makevars

Even still, I'm not sure it would work and you may have to pay for more RAM.

Ben

messages.subject: n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.subject_clean: n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.body_plain:
We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is

y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)

where mu is a common intercept, a_i is a random intercept, A is a matrix, and Sigma is a covariance matrix. The observation model for the jth observation at the ith site is

z_j ~ MVN(y_j,Eta)

where Eta is a covariance matrix. There are some time points at which some sites aren't observed (I've skipped over the details of how we match up observations with corresponding true states).

In RStan 2.4.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu, everything seemed to work OK (although I'm sure it's not very efficient code). In RStan 2.5.0, if the warmup is long enough, we get n_eff=1 for all parameters (their values remain constant). Maybe we did something wrong that leads to an overflow or underflow, that in turn causes a gradient problem? And somehow we got away with it in 2.4.0?

R script and stan code attached, along with some example data files (ddatasim.txt, tmatch.txt, yrefs.txt, all needed to run the code) and output of sessionInfo() in R.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill and Krzysztof,

The documentation is incorrect for v2.5.0. This is a known bug, Stan #1096: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1096

And it will be fixed for the next release (TBD).

Daniel

On Mon, Nov 17, 2014 at 3:01 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I recently ran into (I think) this---see Bob's answer: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/tdHs_ZObLoc/6ROfE36YUZUJ
>
>
> On Monday, November 17, 2014 2:24:06 PM UTC-5, Bill Gillespie wrote:
> > I was attempting to take advantage of overloading of user-defined functions. In particular I tried to define functions with the following signatures:
> >
> >   matrix twoCptModel(real[] time, real[] amt, real[] rate, int[] cmt, int[] evid,
> >     real[] CL, real[] Q, real[] V1, real[] V2, real[] ka, int ntMax)
> >
> >   matrix twoCptModel(real[] time, real[] amt, real[] rate, int[] cmt, int[] evid,
> >     real CL, real Q, real V1, real V2, real ka, int ntMax)
> >
> > That resulted in a compile time error indicating a non-allowable function redefinition. Apparently functions in which the arguments differ only by real vs real[] cannot be overloaded. I confirmed this with the toy functions:
> >
> >   real test1(real x){
> >     return x;
> >   }
> >
> >   real test1(real[] x){
> >     return x[1];
> >   }
> >
> > They resulted in the error message:
> >
> > Error in compileCode(f, code, language = language, verbose = verbose) :
> >   Compilation ERROR, function(s)/method(s) not created! file4623cde85c6.cpp:304:8: error: redefinition of 'test1_functor__'
> > struct test1_functor__ {
> >        ^
> > file4623cde85c6.cpp:283:8: note: previous definition is here
> > struct test1_functor__ {
> >        ^
> >
> > This is not too hard to work around, but the ability to overload functions that differ in this way would be nice.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Bill
> >

messages.body_plain:
I may have done some progress.

First, I attempted to compile 2.4.0 but I got the same type of errors.

Looking around I have found that this type of error was quite common when MS started to include their <stdint.h>

In brief, I got a successful compilation of 2.5.0.1 with this 3 simple steps:
1. substitution of folder with Boost_1.54.00 with Boost_1.55.0
2. addition of /EHsc (not /Ehsc as reported here: http://pystan.readthedocs.org/en/readthedocs/windows.html) to 'extensions_extra_compile_args'
3. modification at 'stack_alloc.hpp', row 8 to read: #if _MSC_VER < 1600

After that, I got another issue.. using the example code reported on PyPi, I realized that Python extension must be created with the same compiler as Python.

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

[I'm splitting out your email. It doesn't really relate to the other thread.]

Which instructions did you follow on which website?

It looks like you're using gcc to compile PyStan, which isn't going to work. Are you just trying to install PyStan? Or install it under specific compiler, anaconda release? Or something more customized?

It looks like you're using the tool chain provided by Rtools. A few points:
- PyStan won't compile under gcc, you'll need to use g++.
- even if you used g++ from RTools, it's not going to work with the debug flag, "-g". This is a Windows RTools g++ specific limitation.
- looks like you've got MSVC specific flags in there as well. Are you trying to use MSVC or g++? Or does it not matter as long as it works?

Daniel

messages.subject: State of PyStan on Windows
messages.subject_clean: State of PyStan on Windows
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

If you're interested in using PyStan for Windows your best bet is to use
Anaconda Python 2.7 and use the precompiled version of PyStan (2.4.0.3,
I believe). We're working on a new release.

Here are the steps to install PyStan on Windows:

- Install Anaconda Python 2.7
- Install and configure Visual Studio 2008 Express, using these instructions: https://github.com/menpo/menpo/wiki/%5BDevelopment-Windows%5D-Setting-up-a-development-environment
- Install PyStan via conda: conda install -c patricksnape pystan

That's it! PyStan should work at this point.

If you've found another reproducible way to install and use PyStan on Windows,
please get in touch (preferably via stan...@googlegroups.com). It would be
great to hear about your experience.

Thanks,

Allen

On Friday, 14 November 2014 17:27:08 UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> That's exactly what the problem is.  Cranking down the
> step size will stop you from accidentally jumping too far
> into stiff regions of parameter space, assuming the high
> mass regions are not stiff and you can get from the initialization
> point to the high mass region without encountering stiffness.
>

Even when constraining the parameters of my PK model, increasing the acceptance rate (0.98) and decreasing the step size (0.008), sampling is extremely slow for my problem (24h for just 200 iterations). The results are consistent with those obtained with the analytical solution of the model though.
I'm surprised since the model is simple (2 states) and the amount of PK data that I analysed is not big (30 individuals). I've attached the program that I use. Am I doing something wrong?

--
Thierry

messages.body_plain:
[changed subject]

Stan is currently on Boost 1.54, because of restrictions
on size imposed by CRAN (the R repository); 5MB is too
large for them.  We're not on CRAN yet, but Ben and Jiqiang
are working on it.

Boost finally got 1.57 out, so we're now several versions
behind.

We may wind up upgrading the Boost libs in everything but
RStan in the next release.

I don't know about PyStan, but in both RStan and CmdStan,
you can specify your own Boost lib paths.  I don't think
anyone's tested beyond 1.54, though, so you'd be on your
own with that.

- Bob

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I think you should be able to get rstan working. If the computer in question has the prerequistes --- Rtools and the Rcpp package (which is best installed from source) plus the R packages BH, RcppEigen, inline, KernSmooth (which can be installed from binaries) --- then you should be able to download https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/releases/download/v2.5.0/rstan_2.5.0.tar.gz on an unsecured computer and copy it to the in computer in question. Then execute in R

install.packages(file.path("path", "to", "rstan_2.5.0.tar.gz"), type = "source")

which will try to install rstan from (for example) C:\path\to\rstan_2.5.0.tar.gz .

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5.0 (but not in 2.4.0)
messages.body_plain:
I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
the problem.

For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
parameters.

We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.

As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).

If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
<lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
a normal density such as

  normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);

For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
to the constraint).

- Bob

> On Nov 17, 2014, at 12:54 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
>
> y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)
>
> where mu is a common intercept, a_i is a random intercept, A is a matrix, and Sigma is a covariance matrix. The observation model for the jth observation at the ith site is
>
> z_j ~ MVN(y_j,Eta)
>
> where Eta is a covariance matrix. There are some time points at which some sites aren't observed (I've skipped over the details of how we match up observations with corresponding true states).
>
> In RStan 2.4.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu, everything seemed to work OK (although I'm sure it's not very efficient code). In RStan 2.5.0, if the warmup is long enough, we get n_eff=1 for all parameters (their values remain constant). Maybe we did something wrong that leads to an overflow or underflow, that in turn causes a gradient problem? And somehow we got away with it in 2.4.0?
>
> R script and stan code attached, along with some example data files (ddatasim.txt, tmatch.txt, yrefs.txt, all needed to run the code) and output of sessionInfo() in R.
>

I find it useful to plot a histogram of Rhat, and n_eff / total sample
in rstan, and then eyeball it for outliers (for long vectors, the plot
is not always informative since it only shows the first few values).

I found that I could extract Rhat and n_eff using

summary(fit)$summary[,"Rhat"]
summary(fit)$summary[,"n_eff"]

and the total sample size using

length(extract(fit, pars = "lp__")[[1]])

from a stanfit object `fit`, so I can do what I need, but I am wondering

1. if there is a method in the API, and if yes, what it is (the above
seems so ad hoc that I am sure I am missing something)

2. if not, are there plans to include a few convenience functions?

Best,

Tamas

"Rstan" is a typo on the webpage.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running a model where n_eff is, for 99% of the parameters, equal to
the size of the posterior sample. This sounds too good to believe,
should I suspect something strange here? I devoted some thought to
coding the model in Stan (including some transformations), but this is
the first time I get so perfect sampling for a nontrivial model, so I
thought I would ask (I know that Stan is great, not questioning that
:D).

I ran the model on simulated data and everything is correctly estimated.

The exceptions are lp__ and three other variables, where n_eff is about
30-50% of the sample size, which is still great. Rhat is very good too.

Best,

Tamas

Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
messages.body_plain:
If you're using multiple diffuse random initializations and consistently getting good n_eff/Rhat and reliable estimation on simulated data then you're probably fine (and fortunate to have a nice model!).  The only major concern for me would be missed multimodality but if you're using multiple diffuse initializations then that should get caught by Rhat.  A potential secondary concern would be if the adaptation was too conservative and consequently you were only exploring a small part of the space and not capture variance and tail behaviour well, but again that would get picked up with multiple diffuse initializations.

So, in summary, confirm that you're using multiple diffuse starts (with different random seeds!) and then remember that Stan is awesome :)

Cheers,
Marcus

Hi -

I'm currently working on a model predicting an individual's laboratory-confirmed diagnosis with a disease from a vector of binary symptom indicators and continuous age.

My implementation is essentially the same as the vanilla GP implementation on page 130 of the Stan reference (hence the lack of a code example). However, since certain symptoms may be less important to the lab-confirmed diagnosis than others, I have been trying to implement the automatic relevance determination on page 133 of the reference manual. When I try to do this, however, the parameter values tend to blow up. So, I was wondering if anyone out there with experience working with these kinds of models had a suggestion for a) priors for the relevance parameters and/or b) constraints that might make for a more useful model.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

-Jon Zelner

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
messages.body_plain:
If you have a t with low df, the whole “effective sample size” notion has problems, as we’ve defined it, because it’s based on means and variances.  If you really want to get weird answers, try a Cauchy!

> On Nov 20, 2014, at 2:04 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> A perfect n_eff is an overestimate, but hopefully not a bad overestimate. So, you are probably fine, although we can construct examples where it is not totally fine despite no divergent transitions. One such example is drawing from a multivariate t distribution with sufficiently large K (like 30) and sufficiently small degrees of freedom (like 5). The reason is that there is essentially no autocorrelation marginally but a lot of cross-parameter dependence due to the heavy tails.

> On Nov 20, 2014, at 9:44 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi Bob
>
> Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. That did sound as though it might be the issue, but turns out it didn't make much difference. The others will take a bit more effort. I'm sure they will make the code more efficient, but I also think that it may be changes to multivariate error checking that are the main reason why we get n_eff=1 for all parameters in STAN 2.5, but not 2.4. I've attached representative trace plots for four of the parameters, under both versions. These have the same pseudorandom number seeds, and it looks like everything is behaving the same for about the first 1800 iterations, and then suddenly the STAN 2.5 version stops changing.
>
> Matt
>
> On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:39:25 AM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
> > tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
> > be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
> > the problem.
> >
> > For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
> > and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
> > needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
> > problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
> > we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > parameters.
> >
> > We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
> > an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.
> >
> > As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
> > the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
> > declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
> > explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
> > is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).
> >
> > If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
> > need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
> > <lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
> > firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
> > a normal density such as
> >
> >   normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);
> >
> > For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
> > the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
> > code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
> > be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
> > define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
> > for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
> > to the constraint).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Nov 17, 2014, at 12:54 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > >
> > > We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
> > >
> > > y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)
> > >
> > > where mu is a common intercept, a_i is a random intercept, A is a matrix, and Sigma is a covariance matrix. The observation model for the jth observation at the ith site is
> > >
> > > z_j ~ MVN(y_j,Eta)
> > >
> > > where Eta is a covariance matrix. There are some time points at which some sites aren't observed (I've skipped over the details of how we match up observations with corresponding true states).
> > >
> > > In RStan 2.4.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu, everything seemed to work OK (although I'm sure it's not very efficient code). In RStan 2.5.0, if the warmup is long enough, we get n_eff=1 for all parameters (their values remain constant). Maybe we did something wrong that leads to an overflow or underflow, that in turn causes a gradient problem? And somehow we got away with it in 2.4.0?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for GP 'automatic relevance determination'
messages.body_plain:
“Automatic relevance determination” is just hierarchical modeling, right?

I’m cc-ing Aki on this but my quick thoughts are:  (a) Try picking some reasonable hyperparameters, simulating some fake data, and checking that the fit recovers the true values; (b) If it works with fake data but not with real, try using an informative prior.

> On Nov 20, 2014, at 3:16 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi -
>
> I'm currently working on a model predicting an individual's laboratory-confirmed diagnosis with a disease from a vector of binary symptom indicators and continuous age.
>
> My implementation is essentially the same as the vanilla GP implementation on page 130 of the Stan reference (hence the lack of a code example). However, since certain symptoms may be less important to the lab-confirmed diagnosis than others, I have been trying to implement the automatic relevance determination on page 133 of the reference manual. When I try to do this, however, the parameter values tend to blow up. So, I was wondering if anyone out there with experience working with these kinds of models had a suggestion for a) priors for the relevance parameters and/or b) constraints that might make for a more useful model.
>
> Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
>
> -Jon Zelner
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Priors for GP 'automatic relevance determination'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for GP 'automatic relevance determination'
messages.body_plain:
“Automatic relevance determination” is misleading term, as the rho parameter is related more to the non-linearity than the predictive relevance.

Note also that, rho and eta are weakly identifiable and the ratio of them is better identified and affects the nonlinearity. However it is usual to use independent priors (I don't remember if anyone uses joint prior with dependency).

I usually like to think suitable prior for the length scale l=1/rho. If the length scale is larger than the scale of the data the model is practically linear (wrt the particular covariate) and increasing the length scale does not change the model. Thus you should use a prior which goes down for the larger length scale values. If the length scale is so small that the correlation between data points is zero, then decreasing the length scale further does not change the model. Usually I've had no need to restrict the length scale to go to very small values, but sometimes. I usually use half-t prior for the length scale as a weakly informative prior.

Eta corresponds to how much of the variation is explained by the regression function and has a similar role to the prior variance for linear model weights. Thus we can use same weakly informative priors as in linear models. I often use half-t prior
for eta.

Aki

On Friday, November 21, 2014 12:31:25 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> “Automatic relevance determination” is just hierarchical modeling, right?
>
> I’m cc-ing Aki on this but my quick thoughts are:  (a) Try picking some reasonable hyperparameters, simulating some fake data, and checking that the fit recovers the true values; (b) If it works with fake data but not with real, try using an informative prior.
>
>
> > On Nov 20, 2014, at 3:16 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi -
> >
> > I'm currently working on a model predicting an individual's laboratory-confirmed diagnosis with a disease from a vector of binary symptom indicators and continuous age.
> >
> > My implementation is essentially the same as the vanilla GP implementation on page 130 of the Stan reference (hence the lack of a code example). However, since certain symptoms may be less important to the lab-confirmed diagnosis than others, I have been trying to implement the automatic relevance determination on page 133 of the reference manual. When I try to do this, however, the parameter values tend to blow up. So, I was wondering if anyone out there with experience working with these kinds of models had a suggestion for a) priors for the relevance parameters and/or b) constraints that might make for a more useful model.
> >
> > Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
> >
> > -Jon Zelner

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew

I think the trace plots are right. I only ran one chain in this case. The four traces are four different parameters (the four elements of a 2 x 2 matrix). The warmup period is only shown on the 2.5 version, but it's the same on the 2.4 version (I saved the 2.4 figure using dev.copy2eps, which doesn't support transparency. My postdoc made the 2.5 version on a different computer, and saved it in some other way).

Matt

On Thursday, November 20, 2014 10:31:23 PM UTC, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, these traceplots look wrong.  Shouldn’t each chain be a different color on the plot?
>
> > On Nov 20, 2014, at 9:44 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob
> >
> > Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. That did sound as though it might be the issue, but turns out it didn't make much difference. The others will take a bit more effort. I'm sure they will make the code more efficient, but I also think that it may be changes to multivariate error checking that are the main reason why we get n_eff=1 for all parameters in STAN 2.5, but not 2.4. I've attached representative trace plots for four of the parameters, under both versions. These have the same pseudorandom number seeds, and it looks like everything is behaving the same for about the first 1800 iterations, and then suddenly the STAN 2.5 version stops changing.
> >
> > Matt
> >
> > On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:39:25 AM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
> > > tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
> > > be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
> > > the problem.
> > >
> > > For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
> > > and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
> > > needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
> > > problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
> > > we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > > parameters.
> > >
> > > We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
> > > an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > > chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.
> > >
> > > As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
> > > the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
> > > declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
> > > explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
> > > is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).
> > >
> > > If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
> > > need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
> > > <lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
> > > firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
> > > a normal density such as
> > >
> > >   normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);
> > >
> > > For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
> > > the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
> > > code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
> > > be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
> > > define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
> > > for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
> > > to the constraint).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Nov 17, 2014, at 12:54 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
> > > >
> > > > y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)
> > > >

On Friday, November 21, 2014 10:00:43 AM UTC, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> Hi Andrew
>
> I think the trace plots are right. I only ran one chain in this case. The four traces are four different parameters (the four elements of a 2 x 2 matrix). The warmup period is only shown on the 2.5 version, but it's the same on the 2.4 version (I saved the 2.4 figure using dev.copy2eps, which doesn't support transparency. My postdoc made the 2.5 version on a different computer, and saved it in some other way).
>
> Matt
>
> On Thursday, November 20, 2014 10:31:23 PM UTC, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi, these traceplots look wrong.  Shouldn’t each chain be a different color on the plot?
> >
> > > On Nov 20, 2014, at 9:44 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Bob
> > >
> > > Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. That did sound as though it might be the issue, but turns out it didn't make much difference. The others will take a bit more effort. I'm sure they will make the code more efficient, but I also think that it may be changes to multivariate error checking that are the main reason why we get n_eff=1 for all parameters in STAN 2.5, but not 2.4. I've attached representative trace plots for four of the parameters, under both versions. These have the same pseudorandom number seeds, and it looks like everything is behaving the same for about the first 1800 iterations, and then suddenly the STAN 2.5 version stops changing.
> > >
> > > Matt
> > >
> > > On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:39:25 AM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
> > > > tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
> > > > be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
> > > > the problem.
> > > >
> > > > For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
> > > > and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
> > > > needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
> > > > problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
> > > > we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > > > parameters.
> > > >
> > > > We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
> > > > an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > > > chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.
> > > >
> > > > As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
> > > > the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
> > > > declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
> > > > explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
> > > > is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).
> > > >
> > > > If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
> > > > need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
> > > > <lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
> > > > firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
> > > > a normal density such as
> > > >
> > > >   normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);
> > > >
> > > > For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
> > > > the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
> > > > code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
> > > > be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
> > > > define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
> > > > for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
> > > > to the constraint).
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > On Nov 17, 2014, at 12:54 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
> > > > >
> > > > > y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)
> > > > >
> > > > > where mu is a common intercept, a_i is a random intercept, A is a matrix, and Sigma is a covariance matrix. The observation model for the jth observation at the ith site is
> > > > >
> > > > > z_j ~ MVN(y_j,Eta)
> > > > >
> > > > > where Eta is a covariance matrix. There are some time points at which some sites aren't observed (I've skipped over the details of how we match up observations with corresponding true states).
> > > > >
> > > > > In RStan 2.4.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu, everything seemed to work OK (although I'm sure it's not very efficient code). In RStan 2.5.0, if the warmup is long enough, we get n_eff=1 for all parameters (their values remain constant). Maybe we did something wrong that leads to an overflow or underflow, that in turn causes a gradient problem? And somehow we got away with it in 2.4.0?

(Nota bene: building PyStan *from source* on Windows is currently unsupported.)

Hi Shota,

We did make a patch to Stan so it would support VS2008
(https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/633) and I think we'd be open to any
additional patches that are required. Currently neither Stan nor PyStan requires
C++11 support. In short, I think VS2010 should work if VS2008 works. That said,
there could have been a breaking change in 2.5.0.

We'd love to have someone who has experience with compiling Python extensions on
Windows as part of the PyStan team. Right now the collective extent of our
knowledge is really just this : https://pystan.readthedocs.org/en/latest/windows.html

Thanks,

Allen

Updated code attached (using Bob's suggestion of a normal distribution for initial observations in each time series: didn't fix the problem of n_eff=1 in RStan 2.5 on Ubuntu).

I also installed RStan 2.5 on a machine running 64-bit Windows 7, and this code ran fine (output of sessionInfo() on that computer attached). So either it's a problem that doesn't occur with the Windows version of RStan, or it's just a problem with the installation of RStan 2.5 on one particular Ubuntu machine.

The warmup period is only shown on the 2.5 version, but it's the same on the 2.4 version (I saved the 2.4 figure using dev.copy2eps, which doesn't support transparency. My postdoc made the 2.5 version on a different computer, and saved it in some other way).

> > > > Hi Bob

> > > > Thanks for those suggestions. The only one I've implemented so far is changing the uniform density for y[k] (where firstyear[k]==1 is true) to a normal density (mean 0, standard deviation 10). The uniform density is often used for this kind of model, but a normal with a high standard deviation is also fine. That did sound as though it might be the issue, but turns out it didn't make much difference. The others will take a bit more effort. I'm sure they will make the code more efficient, but I also think that it may be changes to multivariate error checking that are the main reason why we get n_eff=1 for all parameters in STAN 2.5, but not 2.4. I've attached representative trace plots for four of the parameters, under both versions. These have the same pseudorandom number seeds, and it looks like everything is behaving the same for about the first 1800 iterations, and then suddenly the STAN 2.5 version stops changing.
> > > >
> > > > Matt
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:39:25 AM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > I don't know much about this kind of model, but we have been
> > > > > tinkering with the multivariate error checking, so that may
> > > > > be causing problems.  But that's probably not the root cause of
> > > > > the problem.
> > > > >
> > > > > For both statistical efficiency (high n_eff per iteration)
> > > > > and computational efficiency (fast iterations), this model
> > > > > needs to be rewritten with Cholesky factor parameters.  The
> > > > > problem is that we can't literally do that for your model because
> > > > > we don't (yet) have (inverse) Wishart densities with Cholesky-factor
> > > > > parameters.
> > > > >
> > > > > We'd recommend using a correlation matrix parameterization and
> > > > > an LKJ prior on correlation matrixes. There's a section in the regression
> > > > > chapter of the 2.5 manual that explains how to code it.
> > > > >
> > > > > As written, the y[k] where firstyear[k] == 1 will be problematic because
> > > > > the model doesn't provide the same support as the parameter
> > > > > declaration for y, which is unconstrained.  This will kill any trajectory
> > > > > explored by the sampler that moves into a region where the density
> > > > > is 0 (outside min_y and max_y).
> > > > >
> > > > > If you really need that uniform density with limited support, you
> > > > > need to declare a different parameter vector with constraint
> > > > > <lower=min_y,upper=max_y> for the parameters y[k] for which
> > > > > firstyear[k] == 1.  But it'll probably be easier just to put
> > > > > a normal density such as
> > > > >
> > > > >   normal((max_y - min_y)/2, (max_y - min_y)/4);
> > > > >
> > > > > For computational efficiency, the best thing to do would be to use
> > > > > the vector form of all the densities.  It'll probably speed up the
> > > > > code by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on dimensionality.  It'd
> > > > > be a bit tricky with the switch on firstyear[k] == 1 unless you
> > > > > define two local vectors (or even better a separate parameter vectors)
> > > > > for the k such that firstyear[k] == 1;  this is a separate motivation
> > > > > to the constraint).
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob

> > > > > > We're working on a discrete-time multivariate Gaussian state space model, in which we have time series from a number of different sites, with a random intercept for sites. The process model for time t at site i is
> > > > > >
> > > > > > y_{i,t} ~ MVN(mu + a_i + A*y_{i,t-1},Sigma)

messages.subject: Mixture distributions for priors?
messages.subject_clean: Mixture distributions for priors?
messages.body_plain:
I am using Stan to estimate parameters of a covariance function, similar to that given on page 87 of the Stan Users' Guide. This has been very useful for analyzing my data at a fixed point in time.

I would now like to extend it to a simple time-varying case. I expect the covariance function parameters estimated at time t to be similar to those at time t+1, so it would be nice if I could use the posterior distribution for the parameters at time t as a prior for the parameters at time t+1. In general, standard prior distributions that I have used in Stan would not fit the observed parameter posterior distributions well. Instead, I would like to find a kernel density estimate of the posterior distribution at time t (outside Stan), and code it in Stan at time t+1 using a mixture distribution prior. Can mixture distributions be used as priors in Stan? If not, I'd be very interested in other ways of approaching this problem.

messages.body_plain:
In the SHINYstan R package I'm working on (which contains an app for interactively exploring Stan models), I use a function I wrote called
stan_get which takes arguments stanfit and what(as well as optional arguments like pars for restricting the parameters used)  and is used like this

rhats <- stan_get(stanfit, what = "rhat") # returns rhats
q_95 <- stan_get(stanfit, what = "quantile", probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) # returns 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles

etc.

This way you can use one function and just change the what argument instead of having 10 or 20 functions. Right now it can return Rhats, effective samples sizes, total sample size, means, SDs and any combination of quantiles.

I've also written the function so that the what argument allows the same thing to be specified in many different ways, since different people use different conventions. So, for example, all of the following will return the effective sample sizes:

stan_get(stanfit, what = "ess")
stan_get(stanfit, what = "ESS")
stan_get(stanfit, what = "n_eff")
stan_get(stanfit, what = "N_eff")
stan_get(stanfit, what = "neff")
stan_get(stanfit, what = "Neff")

As Bob would say, this should go in the manual…
P.S.  I just taught the birthdays example in class on Thurs and now I have a bunch of questions to ask you about it.

> On Nov 21, 2014, at 2:38 AM, Aki Vehtari <Aki.V...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> “Automatic relevance determination” is misleading term, as the rho parameter is related more to the non-linearity than the predictive relevance.
>
> Note also that, rho and eta are weakly identifiable and the ratio of them is better identified and affects the nonlinearity. However it is usual to use independent priors (I don't remember if anyone uses joint prior with dependency).
>
> I usually like to think suitable prior for the length scale l=1/rho. If the length scale is larger than the scale of the data the model is practically linear (wrt the particular covariate) and increasing the length scale does not change the model. Thus you should use a prior which goes down for the larger length scale values. If the length scale is so small that the correlation between data points is zero, then decreasing the length scale further does not change the model. Usually I've had no need to restrict the length scale to go to very small values, but sometimes. I usually use half-t prior for the length scale as a weakly informative prior.
>
> Eta corresponds to how much of the variation is explained by the regression function and has a similar role to the prior variance for linear model weights. Thus we can use same weakly informative priors as in linear models. I often use half-t prior
> for eta.
>
>
> Aki
>
> On Friday, November 21, 2014 12:31:25 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > “Automatic relevance determination” is just hierarchical modeling, right?
> >
> > I’m cc-ing Aki on this but my quick thoughts are:  (a) Try picking some reasonable hyperparameters, simulating some fake data, and checking that the fit recovers the true values; (b) If it works with fake data but not with real, try using an informative prior.

When I try to do this, however, the parameter values tend to blow up. So, I was wondering if anyone out there with experience working with these kinds of models had a suggestion for a) priors for the relevance parameters and/or b) constraints that might make for a more useful model.

messages.body_plain:
I made a note to put it in the manual.  What was the conclusion on
automatic reslevance determination --- should I describe it as just
another term for hierarhcical modeling (I haven't actually looked at it
in ages).

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-64106940

- Bob

> On Nov 21, 2014, at 10:04 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> As Bob would say, this should go in the manual…
> P.S.  I just taught the birthdays example in class on Thurs and now I have a bunch of questions to ask you about it.
>
>> On Nov 21, 2014, at 2:38 AM, Aki Vehtari <Aki.V...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>>
>> “Automatic relevance determination” is misleading term, as the rho parameter is related more to the non-linearity than the predictive relevance.
>>
>> Note also that, rho and eta are weakly identifiable and the ratio of them is better identified and affects the nonlinearity. However it is usual to use independent priors (I don't remember if anyone uses joint prior with dependency).
>>
>> I usually like to think suitable prior for the length scale l=1/rho. If the length scale is larger than the scale of the data the model is practically linear (wrt the particular covariate) and increasing the length scale does not change the model. Thus you should use a prior which goes down for the larger length scale values. If the length scale is so small that the correlation between data points is zero, then decreasing the length scale further does not change the model. Usually I've had no need to restrict the length scale to go to very small values, but sometimes. I usually use half-t prior for the length scale as a weakly informative prior.
>>
>> Eta corresponds to how much of the variation is explained by the regression function and has a similar role to the prior variance for linear model weights. Thus we can use same weakly informative priors as in linear models. I often use half-t prior
>> for eta.
>>
>>
>> Aki
>>
>> On Friday, November 21, 2014 12:31:25 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> “Automatic relevance determination” is just hierarchical modeling, right?
>>
>> I’m cc-ing Aki on this but my quick thoughts are:  (a) Try picking some reasonable hyperparameters, simulating some fake data, and checking that the fit recovers the true values; (b) If it works with fake data but not with real, try using an informative prior.
>>
>>
>>> On Nov 20, 2014, at 3:16 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi -
>>>
>>> I'm currently working on a model predicting an individual's laboratory-confirmed diagnosis with a disease from a vector of binary symptom indicators and continuous age.
>>>
>>> My implementation is essentially the same as the vanilla GP implementation on page 130 of the Stan reference (hence the lack of a code example). However, since certain symptoms may be less important to the lab-confirmed diagnosis than others, I have been trying to implement the automatic relevance determination on page 133 of the reference manual. When I try to do this, however, the parameter values tend to blow up. So, I was wondering if anyone out there with experience working with these kinds of models had a suggestion for a) priors for the relevance parameters and/or b) constraints that might make for a more useful model.
>>>
>>> Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
>>>
>>> -Jon Zelner

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture distributions for priors? [time series of covariance matrices]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture distributions for priors? [time series of covariance matrices]
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can use mixtures in Stan.  There's a chapter
in the modeling language manual on discrete mixtures and we
discuss some continuous mixture parameterizations in the reparameterization
chapter.

I didn't understand what you meant going on outside Stan.  As
long as it's done ahead of time and passed in as data you can
use it.

You might also try fitting it as a time series, but I don't know
what kind of distributions would be useful there --- Ben and Andrew
probably have advice here.

That would work out to be a stochastic volatility model, but with
covariance matrices, not just variances in the time series.

- Bob

> On Nov 21, 2014, at 4:26 PM, Kaighin McColl <kai...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am using Stan to estimate parameters of a covariance function, similar to that given on page 87 of the Stan Users' Guide. This has been very useful for analyzing my data at a fixed point in time.
>
> I would now like to extend it to a simple time-varying case. I expect the covariance function parameters estimated at time t to be similar to those at time t+1, so it would be nice if I could use the posterior distribution for the parameters at time t as a prior for the parameters at time t+1. In general, standard prior distributions that I have used in Stan would not fit the observed parameter posterior distributions well. Instead, I would like to find a kernel density estimate of the posterior distribution at time t (outside Stan), and code it in Stan at time t+1 using a mixture distribution prior. Can mixture distributions be used as priors in Stan? If not, I'd be very interested in other ways of approaching this problem.
>
>

I'm a bit puzzled by Aki's response. It would make sense for me, if the dimension of the input (==D) would be one. But if I understood the original question correctly, here we would have:
a) D>1

I mean, if for example rho[1]==0, then we could just drop the first input dimension and we still would get exactly the same results. In general, wouldn't it be true that the closer the rho[d] is to zero the less effect x[,d] would have? (well, the original scale of the inputs matters, so it's not exactly that straightforward unless we normalize the inputs etc)

But maybe I'm missing something here?

3.  “Determination” is just inference.
