messages.body_plain:
This may be related to another problem Daniel and Rob just
tracked down with Ben's help --- we were very strict in our
symmetry conditions for cov_matrix parameters.  We've relaxed
that in a branch, but haven't released the fixed version yet.
So things might work in the current dev branch (I think that
fix got merged).

But what you really want to do is reformulate your model
in terms of a cholesky factor of a correlation matrix rather
than in terms of a cov_matrix parameter W.  There's a section
in the regression chapter of the language manual that works
through an example. We're recommending the LKJ priors on correlation
matrices along with independently scaled variances.

I didn't work through seeing if all the Jacobians got accounted
for in your change of variables for the Wishart (I would've thought
using a loop index in a parameter, as in your chi_square, would be
wrong if I hadn't seen Ben doing it in our transform code).

We have an open feature request to fill in the Wishart and inverse
Wishart for Cholesky factors of covariance matrices, but we don't
have it yet.

There are other improvements you can make for efficiency, but
I'd hang on until the model's working.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Priors for GP 'automatic relevance determination'
messages.subject_clean: Priors for GP 'automatic relevance determination'
messages.body_plain:
> In general, wouldn't it be true that the closer the rho[d] is to zero the less effect x[,d] would have?

A priori yes, but not a posteriori as the actual dependencies between x and y affect also. What I tried to say is that with a covariate x1 having a linear effect and another covariate x2 having a nonlinear effect, it is possible that rho1<rho2 even if the predictive relevance of x1 is higher. The rho is related to the relevance, but it is more accurate to say that it measures the nonlinearity (or the expected number of upcrossings, GPML p. 80). I couldn't quickly find a nice example with GP, but figures 1+3 in http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/LampinenVehtari_NN2001_preprint.pdf illustrate the same issue with MLP. We have made the same experiment with GPs, but just couldn't now find if I have the figures somewhere.

Aki

messages.subject: Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.subject_clean: Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stanimals,

gsim is a new R package to post-process posterior simulations. Its goal is to make it easy to create numerical and graphical summaries involving posterior parameters. In particular, it should  be helpful to perform posterior predictive checking.

In a nutshell, gsim abstracts away all loops over simulations so that the code reflects the math and not technicalities like array instantiation, subsetting, etc. It also provides tools to easily plot fitted models while displaying posterior uncertainty.

The project page is on github: http://github.com/lionelgit/gsim
You will find a tutorial here: https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/239966/gsim.html

I've put in place unit tests to make sure that gsim outputs are reliable, but for the moment you should of course keep an eye on the results and watch out for bugs. I am interested in your comments on the design, potential features, and any issues.

Lionel

This reminds me very much of Jouni Kerman's rv (random variable)
package for R:

  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rv/index.html

The idea is that random vars are represented as simulations and can
be combined by various operations that respects the random variableness,
such as (alpha + beta) doing the right thing (adding simulations
iteration by iteration).

I'm not enough of an R expert to comment on the rest.  For what it's
worth, I don't find the loops that onerous.  A

Within Stan, we're always torn between

 1.  doing the simulations within the generated quantities block, and

 2.  doing them on the outside (doing the loop version of what gsim's doing).

A drawback to (1) is that you have to figure out what you need ahead of time.
But that comes with a benefit that you get all the convergence monitoring
automatically, and things like R-hat and n_eff are sensitive to non-linear transforms.

(2) is complementary to (1) in that you can figure out what you need later,
but then you have to work to get R-hat and n_eff and what not.

The major drawback to (2)  [from a Stan perspective] is that it's done in an
outside language (R, Matlab, Python, etc.), and then you're doing many of the same
calculations as in the original Stan model, but with different syntaxes and perhaps
different parameterizations.

Of course, the benefit of doing something like (2) in an external R package
like gsim is that it'll work for other forms of output than Stan's.

We're having the same issue with how to organize posterior visualizations and
analysis (similar to what Coda does).  We have lots of R developers who want
to write gsim-like packages external to Stan, the most recent example being the
Shiny visualizations discussed on stan-users a week or two ago.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I have a bit of a complicated model:
The response (y_hat) are N pairs of observations coming from I individuals in T treatments, where these I individuals have C covariates.
The data have measurement errors (e_hat) in the response, and each pair of y_hat observations have covariance, which is given as a vector c_hat of length N.

The model quantifies an imbalance effect between the pair of observations per treatment (parameterized by a vector nu_treatment of length T), an individual effect (parameterized by a vector lambda_individual of length I), and the covariate coefficients. It also has an intercept per treatment (parameterized by a vector gamma_treatment of length T).
It therefore puts a hierarchy over nu_treatment, lambda_individual, an error for each treatment (sigma_sq_treatment), and the treatment intercept.

In addition, it is a mixture of two normals at the observation level with mixing proportions delta and 1-delta

In the log-posterior computation statement, called by increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(delta) + multi_normal_log(y_hat, positive_normal_hyper_mean, sigma) , log1m(1-delta) + multi_normal_log(y_hat, negative_normal_hyper_mean, sigma)))

sigma, which is the covariance matrix of the pair of observations. is constructed at each sampling iteration for each observation n E N as:
sigma_sq_treatment+e_hat[n]     ,     c_hat[n]
c_hat[n]     ,     sigma_sq_treatment+e_hat[n]

Calling stan I get a string of errors of this kind:
Error :
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): LDLT_Factor of covariance parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite. LDLT_Factor of covariance parameterlast conditional variance is -13.2475:0.
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

I must be doing something wrong and probably also inefficient as I'm not taking advantage of the cholesky decomposition, but I'm not sure how to implement what's given as examples in the stan manual to my problem.

Thanks a lot,
rubi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] LDLT_Factor of covariance parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite error.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] LDLT_Factor of covariance parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite error.
messages.body_plain:
You need to check that your constructed covariance matrix actually
is positive definite.

> sigma_sq_treatment+e_hat[n]     ,     c_hat[n]
> c_hat[n]     ,     sigma_sq_treatment+e_hat[n]

My linear algebra isn't the strongest, but I think you
need to keep

  c_hat[n] < sigma_sq_treatment + e_hat[n]

That is, there can't be more covariance than the product
of the sds (each of which is the same here by construction).

If this constraint gets violated, the sampler won't be able to move.

We've patched the checks recently, but just for symmetry, which
isn't going to be a problem with your construction.

There's no easy way to do this directly with a Cholesky factor
because you're not estimating a plain correlation or covariance
matrix, but constructing it from pieces.  You could factor the
result by hand (it's only 2 x 2) and use the more efficient Cholesky
parameterization of multi-normal.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the feedback Bob.

> This reminds me very much of Jouni Kerman's rv (random variable) package for R

Yes, gsim was first implemented using a similar object oriented approach. However, this was not flexible and rather slow for complex operations on many simulations. It is not flexible because a generic method is needed for every function and operator to be used with posterior objects. The reactive functions in particular were cumbersome to implement and really slow (they had to precompute a grid of possible values over some range defined ahead of time).

So after reading Wickham's book on R programming I reimplemented everything using a 'computing on the language' approach. This makes gsim fully flexible for any array operations (with some current limitations such as subsetting, but that should work in the future), and much faster. I also may rewrite it in Rcpp in the long term, which would make it faster than using R loops.

> For what it's worth, I don't find the loops that onerous.

Project files quickly become a mess though. I think it's much better when each line of code is a direct translation of a mathematical idea. Also, an important part of gsim is to save snippets of code to be reused with different models. So this package aims to make project files neater and easier to read, as well as more organized.

> Within Stan, we're always torn between
> 1.  doing the simulations within the generated quantities block, and
> 2.  doing them on the outside (doing the loop version of what gsim's doing).

I think it's not so much a tension than an emulation. Model exploration and model checking (which is also exploratory in its nature) are a critical part of bayesian analysis. I don't think that Stan can (nor it should) offer a framework to perform these exploratory tasks.

> The major drawback to (2)  [from a Stan perspective] is that it's done in an outside language (R, Matlab, Python, etc.), and then you're doing many of the same calculations as in the original Stan model, but with different syntaxes and perhaps different parameterizations.

One great thing with Stan is its compatibility with many platforms in which post-processing of simulations and exploration of models take place. gsim is merely an addition to the R platform so that working with simulations is seamless. It does not compete with Stan's generated quantities. Once the exploration is done, the model can be refitted in Stan to obtain convergence diagnostics on critical quantities.

> We're having the same issue

I don't think this is an 'issue' though. Why strive for Stan's compatibility with many frameworks and then be worried that these frameworks develop tools to work with Stan's outputs? As I see it, ShinyStan is only a way of displaying information provided by Stan.

Lionel

messages.body_plain:
Lionel, thanks for writing this! I have been looking for approaches to
posterior predictive checks [1] for a while, since I found rv cumbersome
in practice.

[1] https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/eOf6oOm9xIY/discussion

I looked at gsim briefly and I think your approach is preferable to
overloading the standard operators (like rv does). However, I have to
say that I find the whole non-standard evaluation concept very brittle
in R -- I know that Wickham uses it extensively, but it becomes tricky
when you are trying to do something nontrivial (reuse code, etc).

So for the moment I will continue to use loops -- I don't find them
cumbersome per se, but I think that more abstraction is less
error-prone, but I will follows gsim with interest.

IMO posterior predictive checks can be best conceptualized as mapping
tuples to tuples (lists in R) with a function. A library would help in
extracting the tuples from the posterior for each draw, and then
organizing the results in containers. In R, for efficiency, posteriors
are lists of arrays instead of vectors of lists, so the key is going
back and forth between these two representations, and making sure
variable names are mapped correctly, which is where computing on the
language comes in. I am wondering if the latter could be more
transparent and composable with a bit of extra work on the part of the
user: I imagine something like

map_posterior(function, posterior, inargs, outargs)

where inargs and outargs would be alists (list with names elements in R)
specifying variable names and the corresponding columns, and the
function would do the following:

1. extract a draw from the posterior,
2. arrange the arguments and do_call the function,
3. for the first call, guess dimensions from the list that was returned
and create the containers, for subsequent calls, just check consistency,
4. save the results for that draw,
5. return them at the end.

The benefit of this is that there is no non-standard evaluation, just a
function application. I wrote this in R but it turns out to be
hopelessly slow (in my naive implementation, I am not an R wizard). If
you have a similar core function in gsim, or something that can be
abstracted like this, maybe you could consider exposing it so people
could contribute an alternative interface with standard evaluation.

Best,

Tamas

On Wed, Nov 26 2014, Lionel Henry <lione...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the feedback Bob.
>
>
> This reminds me very much of Jouni Kerman's rv (random variable) package
>> for R
>
>
> Yes, gsim was first implemented using a similar object oriented approach.
> However, this was not flexible and rather slow for complex operations on
> many simulations. It is not flexible because a generic method is needed for
> every function and operator to be used with posterior objects. The reactive
> functions in particular were cumbersome to implement and really slow (they
> had to precompute a grid of possible values over some range defined ahead
> of time).
>
> So after reading Wickham's book on R programming I reimplemented everything
> using a 'computing on the language' approach. This makes gsim fully
> flexible for any array operations (with some current limitations such as
> subsetting, but that should work in the future), and much faster. I also
> may rewrite it in Rcpp in the long term, which would make it faster than
> using R loops.
>
>
> For what it's worth, I don't find the loops that onerous.
>
>
> Project files quickly become a mess though. I think it's much better when
> each line of code is a direct translation of a mathematical idea. Also, an
> important part of gsim is to save snippets of code to be reused with
> different models. So this package aims to make project files neater and
> easier to read, as well as more organized.
>
>
> Within Stan, we're always torn between
>> 1.  doing the simulations within the generated quantities block, and
>> 2.  doing them on the outside (doing the loop version of what gsim's
>> doing).
>
>
> I think it's not so much a tension than an emulation. Model exploration and
> model checking (which is also exploratory in its nature) are a critical
> part of bayesian analysis. I don't think that Stan can (nor it should)
> offer a framework to perform these exploratory tasks.
>
>
> The major drawback to (2)  [from a Stan perspective] is that it's done in
>> an outside language (R, Matlab, Python, etc.), and then you're doing many
>> of the same calculations as in the original Stan model, but with different
>> syntaxes and perhaps different parameterizations.
>
>
> One great thing with Stan is its compatibility with many platforms in which
> post-processing of simulations and exploration of models take place. gsim
> is merely an addition to the R platform so that working with simulations is
> seamless. It does not compete with Stan's generated quantities. Once the
> exploration is done, the model can be refitted in Stan to obtain
> convergence diagnostics on critical quantities.
>
>
> We're having the same issue
>
>
> I don't think this is an 'issue' though. Why strive for Stan's
> compatibility with many frameworks and then be worried that these
> frameworks develop tools to work with Stan's outputs? As I see it,
> ShinyStan is only a way of displaying information provided by Stan.
>
>
> Lionel

messages.body_plain:
Hello Tamas,

I am not sure I undertand well your idea of mapping tuples to tuples. I also tried to think about a way of abstracting ppc in functions, but I had trouble finding a solution that would be both flexible, and easier to read than simply spelling out the checking.

At one point I thought of something like this:

  bernoulli_check(y = switched, p = fitted, stat = sd(y - p))

Well I just went ahead and implemented it :-) See in https://github.com/lionelgit/gsim/blob/master/R/summaries.r.

It only required a handful of tweaks to the expression parser. Besides `y`, `p` and `stat`, it takes a `p_value` argument to indicate whether it should return n_sims p values (the default) or a list containing y and y_rep (returning a list is not 100% clean at the moment because the code that handles listed outputs has not yet been adapted).

This function uses both SE and NSE. The SE part computes replicates. The NSE part takes the 'stat' argument to evaluate it on both y and y_rep, for each simulation.

Here it is in action:

  sims <- gsim(wells_fit, wells_data, n_sims = 200)

  p <- sims({
    X <- cbind(intercept(), c_dist100, c_arsenic, c_dist100 * c_arsenic)
    fitted <- inv_logit(X %*% col_vector(beta))

    bernoulli_check(y = switched, p = fitted, stat = sd(y - p))
  })

It could easily be adapted for other distributions. However I'm not sure how this approach would play out with more complicated checks for hierarchical models etc.

> I find the whole non-standard evaluation concept very brittle in R

At first I also thought that computing on the language to wrap everything into loops before execution would be brittle. However, when I tested a rough implementation, it worked surprisingly well. One thing that helps is that every input is an array or a numeric vector, and that most function used inside gsim operate only on this type of inputs.

> it becomes tricky when you are trying to do something nontrivial (reuse code, etc).

I'm not sure what you mean by something nontrivial and by reusing code. Would quoted snippets fit the use cases you have in mind?

Lionel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Graded Response Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

I was working with examples I found here and I believe that the code posted by Jackson King here contains a mistake. In particular
he declares  real theta[N]; which is incorrect and he intends to have real theta[J];.

Not a biggie but if someone else reads this thread and wants to build from what can be found here it might convenient to have at least this sorted out.

I would appreciate if anyone could comment whether this code is otherwise correct, but as far as I understand I believe this is the case. I compared with the results from grm in the ltm package and the comparison looks great.

Kind regards, Louis

library(ltm)
library(rstan)

data<-Science[c(1,3,4,7)]
data<-cbind(as.numeric(data[,1]),as.numeric(data[,2]), as.numeric(data[,3]), as.numeric(data[,4]) )

c<-4 #Number of categories per item (here, 4)
J<-length(data[,1])
K<-length(data[1,])
N<-J*K
jj<-rep(c(1:J), times=K) #Index for persons
kk<-rep(c(1:K), each=J) #Index for items
y<-c(data[,1], data[,2], data[,3], data[,4])

dat<-list(N=N,
          c=c,
          J=J,
          K=K,
          jj=jj,
          kk=kk,
          y=y
)

grm_code<-"
data {
int<lower=0> N; //Number of observations
int<lower=1> c; //Number of categories
int<lower=1> J; //Number of ids
int<lower=1> K; //Number of items
int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N]; //Identifier
int<lower=1, upper=J> kk[N]; //question
int y[N];  //Data
}
parameters {

real theta[J];

ordered[c-1] tau[K]; //Difficulty
real<lower=0> alpha[K];// discrimination parameter for each item
}
model{
alpha~cauchy(0, 5);
theta~normal(0,1);
for (p in 1:4){
tau[p, 1]~uniform(-100, tau[p, 2]);
tau[p, 2]~uniform(tau[p, 1], tau[p, 3]);
tau[p, 3]~uniform(tau[p, 2], 100);
}
for (n in 1:N)
y[n]~ordered_logistic(alpha[kk[n]]*theta[jj[n]], tau[kk[n]]);
}
"

fit <- stan(model_code = grm_code,

            data = dat, iter = 300, warmup=100, chains =3)

####Some Code to extract abilities from Stan###

s <- extract(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE, permuted=FALSE)
s1 <- s[,1,] #order of parameters as in parameter declaration; ends with _lp
s2 <- s[,2,]
s3 <- s[,3,]
stot <- rbind(s1,s2,s3)

summaryFunc <- function(x, q = c(0.025, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.975)){
  quantile(x,q)
}

stot.summary.standard <- t(apply(stot,2,summaryFunc))
abilities.stan <- stot.summary.standard[1:392,3]

####Use the ltm package####
grm1 <- grm(data, IRT.param=FALSE)
scoresgrm1 <- factor.scores(grm1, resp.patterns=data)[[1]]
abilities <- scoresgrm1[,7]

####Compare#####
plot(abilities, abilities.stan)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Graded Response Model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Graded Response Model
messages.body_plain:
No, that code's still problematic.

With

  parameters {

    ordered[c-1] tau[K]; //Difficulty

it's not consistent to have:

  model {

    for (p in 1:4) {

      tau[p, 1] ~ uniform(-100, tau[p, 2]);
      tau[p, 2] ~ uniform(tau[p, 1], tau[p, 3]);

      tau[p, 3] ~ uniform(tau[p, 2], 100);

because the support in the model is less than that declared
on the parameters.  The declaration allows tau[k,1] to take on
any real value, so it can be less than -100; similarly
tau[k,3] may be greater than 100.

You can use improper priors or provide proper priors, but
the support of the prior should be equal to that of the declared
constraints.  The prior support in the model can be greater than
the declared constraint if the truncation is included to match
the declared constraint;  the truncation may be dropped if
the distribution parameters and the truncation point are constant.

The model clearly has a multiplicative non-identifiability in
alpha and theta,  with linear predictor alpha[kk[n]] * theta[jj[n]].

Taking theta ~ normal(0,1) should fix the scale for theta and
identify the model.  There are other ways to identify such models,
such as fixing components --- I described some of them in the manual
chapter on problematic posteriors and mitigating non-identifiabilities.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for these detailed discussions.  It's very helpful.
I hope Andrew reads this because he's thought a lot about these
issues.

I've never used rv, but we also overload all the functions/operators in
Stan to support autodiff, and it's definitely a lot of work to do right.
I had no idea you could do that kind of thing in R for anything other than
some of the OO methods.  Can you overload addition for an R object type?

The portability issue for Stan is whether things will work across
interfaces in R, Python, MATLAB, Julia, etc. (as well as across C++
compilers and operating system and hardware configs).  The main advantages
to working directly in our generated quantities block is that:

  * it's portable across Stan interfaces, and

  * you get vectorization across samples for free.

The latter is what makes Stan variables (other than data) feel like random
variables and thus makes Stan feel like a probabilistic programming language.
This is the same feel I get from rv and gsim (though I haven't used either),
as well as from BUGS and JAGS, the obvious influences on our language.

The downside for generated quantities is that

  * it only works for Stan, and

  * it requires the posterior analysis to be done along with the fit.

The latter's mainly an issue for flexibility, though it has the advantage
of making things like convergence monitoring integrated.

When we add all of the MLE functions lm(), glm(), MML functions lmer(), glmer(),
and Bayesian MML functions blmer(), and bglmer() directly to Stan (with
wrappers for the lm/lmer expression language in Stan's R package), there'll be
less motivation for anyone to use any other package :-)  We already do MLE
and I'm guessing MML will land in the next six or nine months now that we
have both Rob and Marcus working on it.

What Stan users have been asking us for is something that makes it possible
to use one model for both estimation and simulation.  Unlike
Stan isn't a pure directed graphical modeling language, and it compiles
code dedicated for its inferential task.  This makes the code a lot faster,
but it has the enormous drawback of requiring users to write
two models where BUGS/JAGS would only require one.  There is the bright
side that each model is easier to read for intent, but that's a separate
matter.

- Bob

> On Nov 26, 2014, at 8:41 AM, Lionel Henry <lione...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello Tamas,
>
> I am not sure I undertand well your idea of mapping tuples to tuples. I also tried to think about a way of abstracting ppc in functions, but I had trouble finding a solution that would be both flexible, and easier to read than simply spelling out the checking.
>
> At one point I thought of something like this:
>
>   bernoulli_check(y = switched, p = fitted, stat = sd(y - p))
>
> Well I just went ahead and implemented it :-) See in https://github.com/lionelgit/gsim/blob/master/R/summaries.r.
>
> It only required a handful of tweaks to the expression parser. Besides `y`, `p` and `stat`, it takes a `p_value` argument to indicate whether it should return n_sims p values (the default) or a list containing y and y_rep (returning a list is not 100% clean at the moment because the code that handles listed outputs has not yet been adapted).
>
> This function uses both SE and NSE. The SE part computes replicates. The NSE part takes the 'stat' argument to evaluate it on both y and y_rep, for each simulation.
>
> Here it is in action:
>
>   sims <- gsim(wells_fit, wells_data, n_sims = 200)
>
>   p <- sims({
>     X <- cbind(intercept(), c_dist100, c_arsenic, c_dist100 * c_arsenic)
>     fitted <- inv_logit(X %*% col_vector(beta))
>
>     bernoulli_check(y = switched, p = fitted, stat = sd(y - p))
>   })
>
> It could easily be adapted for other distributions. However I'm not sure how this approach would play out with more complicated checks for hierarchical models etc.
>
>
> > I find the whole non-standard evaluation concept very brittle in R
>
> At first I also thought that computing on the language to wrap everything into loops before execution would be brittle. However, when I tested a rough implementation, it worked surprisingly well. One thing that helps is that every input is an array or a numeric vector, and that most function used inside gsim operate only on this type of inputs.
>
>
> > it becomes tricky when you are trying to do something nontrivial (reuse code, etc).
>

>
>

messages.body_plain:
Just to add to what Bob said:  One thing we’ve been talking about is R or Python wrapper for Stan that does graphical models.  The idea is that we’d create some sort of graphical modeling language and then the wrapper would take that model, along with a choice of which random variables are being specified as data and which are unknown, and then it would write a Stan program, putting the appropriate code into the model and generated quantities blocks.  This would facilitate fake-data simulation and posterior predictive checking, which are two things we want to be doing all the time.

A

P.S.  For an example of what is and is not a graphical model, consider the following 2 lines of Stan code:

theta ~ normal(0,1);
theta ~ normal(0,1);

[Or, how I’d prefer it written:
normal(theta|0,1);
normal(theta|0,1);]

This code, although it looks like two specifications of a prior for theta, is actually in Stan just two contributions to the log-posterior, and it is mathematically equivalent to:

theta ~ normal(0,1/sqrt(2));
[or, as I’d prefer, normal(theta|0,1/sqrt(2));]

> On Nov 26, 2014, at 2:42 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for these detailed discussions.  It's very helpful.
> I hope Andrew reads this because he's thought a lot about these
> issues.
>
> I've never used rv, but we also overload all the functions/operators in
> Stan to support autodiff, and it's definitely a lot of work to do right.
> I had no idea you could do that kind of thing in R for anything other than
> some of the OO methods.  Can you overload addition for an R object type?
>
> The portability issue for Stan is whether things will work across
> interfaces in R, Python, MATLAB, Julia, etc. (as well as across C++
> compilers and operating system and hardware configs).  The main advantages
> to working directly in our generated quantities block is that:
>
>  * it's portable across Stan interfaces, and
>
>  * you get vectorization across samples for free.
>
> The latter is what makes Stan variables (other than data) feel like random
> variables and thus makes Stan feel like a probabilistic programming language.
> This is the same feel I get from rv and gsim (though I haven't used either),
> as well as from BUGS and JAGS, the obvious influences on our language.
>
> The downside for generated quantities is that
>
>  * it only works for Stan, and
>
>  * it requires the posterior analysis to be done along with the fit.
>
> The latter's mainly an issue for flexibility, though it has the advantage
> of making things like convergence monitoring integrated.
>
> When we add all of the MLE functions lm(), glm(), MML functions lmer(), glmer(),
> and Bayesian MML functions blmer(), and bglmer() directly to Stan (with
> wrappers for the lm/lmer expression language in Stan's R package), there'll be
> less motivation for anyone to use any other package :-)  We already do MLE
> and I'm guessing MML will land in the next six or nine months now that we
> have both Rob and Marcus working on it.
>
> What Stan users have been asking us for is something that makes it possible
> to use one model for both estimation and simulation.  Unlike
> Stan isn't a pure directed graphical modeling language, and it compiles
> code dedicated for its inferential task.  This makes the code a lot faster,
> but it has the enormous drawback of requiring users to write
> two models where BUGS/JAGS would only require one.  There is the bright
> side that each model is easier to read for intent, but that's a separate
> matter.
>
> - Bob

algebra can break down.

I didn't want to subvert the stan-users thread, so I started
a new one.

It'd be trivial to add

  foo(y | theta1, ..., thetaK)

as an alternative syntax for

And we can deprecate the latter, though it'll be a bit of
work changing everything, since the syntax is involved in almost
every single model we've written or a user's written.

a function application) and thus evaluating to a value without
side effects, so it may be confusing just using it as a bare statement
that implicitly increments the total log density.

> No, that code's still problematic.
>
> With
>
>   parameters {
>     ordered[c-1] tau[K]; //Difficulty
>
> it's not consistent to have:
>
>   model {
>     for (p in 1:4) {
>       tau[p, 1] ~ uniform(-100, tau[p, 2]);
>       tau[p, 2] ~ uniform(tau[p, 1], tau[p, 3]);
>       tau[p, 3] ~ uniform(tau[p, 2], 100);
>
> because the support in the model is less than that declared
> on the parameters.  The declaration allows tau[k,1] to take on
> any real value, so it can be less than -100; similarly
> tau[k,3] may be greater than 100.
>
> You can use improper priors or provide proper priors, but
> the support of the prior should be equal to that of the declared
> constraints.  The prior support in the model can be greater than
> the declared constraint if the truncation is included to match
> the declared constraint;  the truncation may be dropped if
> the distribution parameters and the truncation point are constant.
>
> The model clearly has a multiplicative non-identifiability in
> alpha and theta,  with linear predictor alpha[kk[n]] * theta[jj[n]].
>
> Taking theta ~ normal(0,1) should fix the scale for theta and
> identify the model.  There are other ways to identify such models,
> such as fixing components --- I described some of them in the manual
> chapter on problematic posteriors and mitigating non-identifiabilities.

> Dear Bob,

> -I thought it is ok to put a restriction on the declaration and have an unrestricted prior
> e.g.
> declare real<lower=0> alpha[K]
> and later on
> alpha~cauchy(0, 2);
>
> but the opposite is not ok?
> No restriction in the declaration but specifying a prior with some restriction e.g. uniform(a,b)  ?

That is correct. If the parameters end up outside of the support of the uniform distribution, the log probability is -inf and there is no gradient. So, NUTS / HMC stops working efficiently. There is a chance it stumbles back into an area of support, but I think our implementation won't.

By default, when Stan initializes its parameters, it chooses random values on the unconstrained scale. If the initial parameters evaluate to a -inf log probability calculation, Stan will choose a different random starting point. It does this a max of 100 times then quits if it can't find a reasonable starting value.

If you're insistent on using that sort of construction, you could start sampling by providing initial values, but it would still be very inefficient. Stan does a change of variables under the hood, which make sampling much easier over bounded variables. There's no possible chance of stepping into a place with no support.

>
> -What would you suggest in the example of above?
> (how would you restrict the ordered declaration if that is the suggestion)

You might be able to do a change of variables yourself and add the right Jacobian term, maybe use a positive ordered, then subtract 100?

I seem to find the source of this behaviour.

Having adapted the rats.stan to my own data, I have seen now that the rat model is composed of many rats with an hyper-parameter on the top hierarchy.

In my test, I had only one single group, so the hyper-parameter was actually not informative.

Removing the hyper-parameter from the model, I managed getting rid of the extremely long auto-correlations.

So my conclusion so far is that too many unnecessary hierarchies might lead to long auto-correlations.

cheers,
s.

On Thursday, November 27, 2014 2:21:31 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> It'd be trivial to add
>
>   foo(y | theta1, ..., thetaK)
>
> as an alternative syntax for
>
>   y ~ foo(theta1, ..., thetaK);
>

> I think of the foo(y|theta) notation as an expression (specifically
> a function application) and thus evaluating to a value without
> side effects, so it may be confusing just using it as a bare statement
> that implicitly increments the total log density.

I don't follow how foo(y|theta) is an expression and y ~ foo(theta) is
not an expression. Neither of them mention the total log density.
To me, the distinction is that the tilde implies simulating draws
from foo(theta). The way to generate a tilde in latex to use $\sim$
suggesting simulation. And in stan models, we are not doing
simulation, but we are really saying that the model should account
for the density foo(y|theta).

I'm not sure what to do about the implicit accumulation of these
densities. But that's a separate question. I think the question is
what can go inside of increment_log_prob(...).

increment_log_prob(y ~ normal(mu,sigma));
increment_log_prob(normal_log(y,mu,sigma));
increment_log_prob(normal_log(y | mu,sigma));

On Wed, Nov 26 2014, Lionel Henry <lione...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am not sure I undertand well your idea of mapping tuples to tuples. I
> also tried to think about a way of abstracting ppc in functions, but I had
> trouble finding a solution that would be both flexible, and easier to read
> than simply spelling out the checking.

Hi Lionel,

Sorry for not being clear. Here is stylized code for what I have in
mind, using the speed of light example from BDA (2nd ed, Chapter 6):

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
y <- is_the_data

my_statistic <- function(y, mu) {
  y_sorted <- sort(y)
  abs(y_sorted[61]-mu)-abs(y_sorted[6]-mu)
}

my_rep <- function(mu, sigma) {
  rnorm(length(y), mu, sigma)
}

## with a loop
M <- length(posterior$mu)
T_data <- numeric(M)
T_sim <- numeric(M)
for (i in 1:M) {
  T_data[i] <- my_statistic(y, posterior$mu[i])
  T_sim[i] <- my_statistic(my_rep(posterior$mu[i], posterior$sigma[i]),
                           posterior$mu[i])
}

## with a hypothetical function map_posterior
map_posterior(function(mu, sigma) {
  list(T_data = my_statistic(y, mu),
       T_sim = my_statistic(my_rep(mu, sigma), mu))
},
              posterior,
              list(mu = "mu", sigma = "sigma")) # input mapping, may not be necessary
## result is a data frame with two columns.
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

map_posterior would take care of calling the function with each draw in
the posterior, and collecting the results etc. I find functional
approaches very clean.

>> I find the whole non-standard evaluation concept very brittle in R
>
> At first I also thought that computing on the language to wrap everything
> into loops before execution would be brittle. However, when I tested a
> rough implementation, it worked surprisingly well. One thing that helps is
> that every input is an array or a numeric vector, and that most function
> used inside gsim operate only on this type of inputs.
>
>
>> it becomes tricky when you are trying to do something nontrivial (reuse
> code, etc).
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by something nontrivial and by reusing code.
> Would quoted snippets fit the use cases you have in mind?

As you mention in the documentation, control flow does not work for
gsim, but I don't know if this is an inherent limitation.

I usually run into problems where I have functions that call functions
which have nonstandard evaluation, since it is hard to parametrize the
latter (Wickham has, of course, packages that work around this, like
lazyeval). But this is not super-relevant for posterior predictive
checks I guess.

Best,

Tamas

You are right. The model without hierarchy is not identifiable, that is, you can get the same or almost the same likelihood with different parameter combinations. In the model, sigma_y and alpha have identical roles, and beta also has two normal components through mu_beta. The peaky priors for variance may also somehow contribute. The likelihood landscape then becomes difficult for the sampler: either very stretched out on some directions (not corresponding to single parameters), or maybe the curvature varies a lot.

NUTS requires some care with respect to this kind of issues.

The stepsize_jitter parameter (see manual) may help if one cannot improve the model.

I would like to constrain one vector of a matrix or 2-d array to be positive, but leave the other vector unconstrained.

This is for a factor analysis model that is parameterized as a hierarchical linear model (i.e., like an IRT model, with manifest variables stacked in "long" format). In particular, I would like to constrain the factor loadings / slopes to be positive to deal with reflection invariance, but let the intercepts be positive or negative.

I also want the intercepts and slopes to be bound as a matrix (or 2-d array) so I can model their correlation using the code from pg 54 of the current stan manual. Looking at that code, the matrix in question is beta.

Any idea how I might go about doing this?

messages.subject: bad mixing and misestimation for Dirichlet hyperprior
messages.subject_clean: bad mixing and misestimation for Dirichlet hyperprior
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on a problem where I noticed that estimating using
simulated data does not deliver a good posterior. I have simplified to a
simple self-contained example below, in the hope that someone can point
out the error I made. The problem is complex because of censoring.

I have N individuals, for each of them I have

1. a data point m,

2. a parameter pair (alpha,beta) which are the first two values from a
simplex (I parametrize this as Dirichlet, not essential to what I am
doing but seemed natural),

3. a parameter w, drawn from a known distribution (for simplicity here),

4. a binomially distributed observation, with probability beta/(1-alpha).

The sample only contains variables for which m/w < (1-alpha)/alpha.

(alpha,beta,w) are interesting to me for each individual, the rest are
nuisance parameters.

To capture the constraint, I obtain w with a transformation from a [0,1]
interval, correcting for the Jacobian. I attach the code for generating
the data and checking the posterior (in R, with plots etc), and the Stan
model.

My problems are

1. that the alpha's are mis-estimated, they all seem to be around the
same value for everyone,

2. the a parameters of the hyperprior for (alpha,beta,_) have bad
mixing, especially the first Dirichlet parameter.

Maybe these are related. Any hints on what I am doing wrong would be
appreciated. I don't think this is a Stan bug, rather user error, but I
can't find the source of it.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

> I had no idea you could do that kind of thing in R for anything
> other than some of the OO methods. Can you overload addition for an
> R object type?

Yes, most operators are generic functions so you can specify methods
for them. Actually, the main OO systems in R (S3 and S4) are based on
overloading generics. The methods do not belong to classes but to
generic functions. Dispatching then takes place based on the class of
the first argument (S3), or based on the classes of the arguments of
the method (S4).

You can also entirely overwrite addition. In R everything is a
function, even operators, so if your new addition function has scoping
precedence, it will prevail.

>  We already do MLE and I'm guessing MML will land in the next six
> or nine months now that we have both Rob and Marcus working on it.

Awesome news!

functions to display fitted lines with posterior uncertainty.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tamas,

Thanks for the example. My function bernoulli_check is not very
different from your idea. The interface uses NSE for the statistic
function, but you can still define and use your own external statistic
functions. So maybe that meets your idea of a 'functional' solution?

By the way, I uploaded normal_check on Github. I also tweaked both
checking functions to make them independent of gsim. This was easy
because gsim uses the same data structure than Stan's extracted
parameters. So now you can directly use them with simulations
extracted from a stanfit.

I also changed the output of these functions. They now return a list
with `y_stat` and `y_rep_stat` with the p-value recorded as an
attribute. I think it's better to have the list returned by default
because checking the test graphically requires the statistics. And the
p-value is still easy to access because I provide a getter function
called `p`: p_value <- p(my_check).

So, for the speed of light example, you would use it as follows:

sims <- extract(speed_stanfit)

symmetry_check <- normal_check(
  y = newcomb, mu = sims$theta, sigma = sims$sigma,
  stat = {
    sorted_y <- sort(y)
    abs(sorted_y[61] - mu) - abs(sorted_y[6] - mu)
  })

p(symmetry_check)

Of course you can just use stat = symmetry_stat(y, mu) if you have
already defined one. And to make everything a bit nicer, you can use
the %$% operator from the package magrittr to expose the data and the
parameters to normal_check (equivalent to use the `with`
function). Then it would be:

symmetry_check <- c(sims, list(y = newcomb)) %$%
  normal_check(y, mu = theta, sigma, stat = symmetry_stat(y, mu))

The problem with the current implementation of these checking
functions is that you can only operate on the parameters of the
data distribution. So, for normal_check, the stat can only depend on
mu and sigma. Does someone has an example of a checking stat that
depends on other parameters than those of the data distribution?

I thought of this issue while I was thinking of a more generic
model_check() that would take y and y_rep as inputs. I thought this
checking function would be useful for the common case where the
replicates are generated with Stan. But a checking function that
cannot operate on any parameters is actually not so practical :-).

However I could make it work inside gsim. Having:

sims(
  model_check(y, y_rep, my_stat(y, theta))
)

is a bit nicer than:

sims({
  y_stat <- my_stat(y, theta)
  y_rep_stat <- my_stat(y_rep, theta)

  list(y_stat, y_rep_stat)
})

Lionel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling statement syntax
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] sampling statement syntax
messages.body_plain:
Syntactically, in a programming language, expressions denote
values and statements denote actions.

So

  sin(x + 3)

is an expression, whereas

  y = sin(x + 3);

is a statement.

Languages like C like to overload things, so that the above statement
may be used as an expression with value sin(x + 3).  Similarly, the expression
may be used as a no-op statement, though no reason to do that if there are no
side effects.

You can see how the distinction's made in Stan in the reference
section of the manual, which has separate chapters on statements
and expressions, as well as the BNF syntax for the language which
has the precise syntactic definition.

All I was trying to say is that foo(y|theta) "feels" more like
an expression to me.

- Bob

> I think of the foo(y|theta) notation as an expression (specifically
> a function application) and thus evaluating to a value without
> side effects, so it may be confusing just using it as a bare statement
> that implicitly increments the total log density.
>
> I don't follow how foo(y|theta) is an expression and y ~ foo(theta) is
> not an expression. Neither of them mention the total log density.
> To me, the distinction is that the tilde implies simulating draws
> from foo(theta). The way to generate a tilde in latex to use $\sim$

> simulation, but we are really saying that the model should account

> and a normal prior on beta.
>
> Now it may not be a good modeling idea, but that's a separate
> issue.
>
> And it won't work if the constraints on alpha depend on beta,
> but here they don't.

It depends on what Christopher intended when he miswrote this "double prior" thing

> model{
>   alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
>   beta ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     Beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_Beta, Sigma_Beta);
> }

If you get rid of the multi_normal() statement, then Bob's normal and half-normal prior remains. If you get rid of the two normal() statements, then you get a wrong, untruncated prior. Multivariate normal priors are typical in this literature, so that is what I was assuming he really meant. Stan doesn't have a truncated multivariate normal distribution, but if only one dimension is inequality constrained, then you can get by with a (possibly multivariate) normal on the unconstrained dimension(s) and a univariate truncated conditional normal distribution on the constrained dimension.

Ben

> On Nov 27, 2014, at 8:06 AM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> You are right. The model without hierarchy is not identifiable, that is, you can get the same or almost the same likelihood with different parameter combinations. In the model, sigma_y and alpha have identical roles, and beta also has two normal components through mu_beta. The peaky priors for variance may also somehow contribute. The likelihood landscape then becomes difficult for the sampler: either very stretched out on some directions (not corresponding to single parameters), or maybe the curvature varies a lot.
>
> NUTS requires some care with respect to this kind of issues.

So does Gibbs!  It's just that Gibbs can move slowly enough that
you don't notice the problem.  There's a chapter in the Stan manual
on problematic posteriors that discusses these issues and compares
HMC with Gibbs (and maybe Metropolis --- I can't recall offhand).

I should add some discussion of hierarchical models without
replicates, because then you run into the problems you mention.

> The stepsize_jitter parameter (see manual) may help if one cannot improve the model.

We're more inclined to recommend stepping up target acceptance
rate from 0.8 and stepping down the initial stepsize.  Both will
help models avoid getting stuck by making the Hamiltonian simulation
follow the curvature in the posterior more closely.  Getting stuck
happens when the step size is too big and the linear approximation
based on the gradient steps too far to accept a proposal --- same as
with too large a step size in Metropolis.

- Bob

messages.subject: Using RStan with knitr
messages.subject_clean: Using RStan with knitr
messages.body_plain:
In some previous threads there’s been questions of how best to use Rstan in knitr documents. Generally people will write the Stan model as a string, and pass that string to the stan function using the model_code argument. However, another (and in my option, better) way to do this is to take advantage of language engines in knitr (http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/engines/). With these engines you can write a Stan code in a separate chunk and still use it later. There are a couple of ways of doing this
Use the cat engine to write the chunk contents to a file, which you can use with stan or stan_model later.
Use a custom stan engine which will compile the contents of the chunk to a stanmodel object which can be sampled with the sampling method.

For the details and an example of an rmarkdown document which uses these approaches see the example document in https://github.com/jrnold/knitr-stan-example .
​

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Announcing gsim 0.1
messages.body_plain:
> The problem with the current implementation of these checking
> functions is that you can only operate on the parameters of the data
> distribution.

Ok, this was actually easy enough to make the checking functions able
to operate on any parameters. I had to add a `params` argument. The
tricky part internally (and also the speed bottleneck) was to find a
way of subsetting arrays of varying dimensions. With this I could
implement `check_model()`. Note that I renamed all checking functions
from *_check to check_* to make them verbs.

So now the global idea behind the checking functions is that you apply
a statistic on both y and y_rep. If you already have y_rep, you call
check_model. If you need to sample replicates, you call the
specialised functions like check_normal or check_bernoulli. Actually,
the distribution-specific functions just sample replicates and then
call check_model themselves.

These functions work outside gsim on extracted stanfit
simulations. (Note that if you need to get simulations in this form,
you can use `as.mclist()` on any object supported in gsim.) They don't
work inside gsim yet, but when they do the only difference will be
that they won't have a params argument.

Example with check_model:

  newcomb_sims <- extract(stanfit)
  out <- check_model(y = radon$y, y_rep, params = newcomb_sims,
    stat = {
      y_sorted <- sort(y)
      abs(y_sorted[61] - y_hat) - abs(y_sorted[6] - y_hat)
    })

Example with check_bernoulli:

  wells_sims <- extract(stanfit)
  out <- check_bernoulli(y = wells$switched, p = y_hat,
    params = wells_sims, stat = sd(y - p)
  )

check_normal is similar to check_bernoulli, only with mu and sigma
arguments.

When params is supplied, NSE is used for the random variables (y_rep,
mu, sigma, p, etc). So if you specify mu = y_hat, they will look
inside params for y_hat. On the other hand, when params is not
supplied, the random variables are obtained from the calling
environment. In both cases, the statistic operates on 'official' param
names (mu, sigma, p), not on supplied names.

I may change that interface if it is confusing. I would love some
feedback from experimented ppc users. One remaining issue is speed,
although it's fast enough for practical purposes. Computing a bernoulli
check on 2000 simulations takes 1.6 seconds on my computer.
Rewriting check_model in c++ would solve this.

Anyway, thanks Tamas. I don't know if these functions would be a good
replacement of map_posterior for you but our discussion helped me see
things more clearly!

Lionel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using RStan with knitr
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using RStan with knitr
messages.body_plain:
Since it may have been unclear what I was saying, I was not suggesting that people write the Stan model in R strings, I was showing ways in which one can write Stan models within a knitr document in their own chunks.  Specifically, I wrote a Stan engine for knitr so (after defining the new engine) you can write a Stan model in a knitr chunk like this:
```{r engine='stan',engine.opts=list(x = "mod")}
parameters {
  real y[2];
}
model {
  y[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
  y[2] ~ double_exponential(0, 2);
}
```
Which will compile the Stan code, and save it to a stanmodel object named mod, which can be used in later chunks, e.g.
```{r}
mod <- sampling(mod)
print(mod)
```
Another way is to write a chunk like this
```{r engine='cat',engine.opts=list(file="foo.stan",lang="stan")}
parameters {
  real y[2];
}
model {
  y[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
  y[2] ~ double_exponential(0, 2);
}
```
This writes the model in a chunk to a file "foo.stan", which can be used later.
```{r}
stan("foo.stan")
```
So, for those who want to (1) use knitr and (2) keep everything in the same document, those are a couple of ways to do it without writing Stan models in R strings.

--
Jeffrey Arnold
University of Washington
Acting Assistant Professor of Political Science
Core Faculty Member of the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using RStan with knitr
messages.body_plain:
I've been playing around with knitr and found I could put the
Stan program in a standalone file with this bit of magic:

```{r, cache.extra = tools::md5sum("soil_incubation_measurement_err.stan")}
fit_me <- stan("soil_incubation_measurement_err.stan",
              data=c("totalC_t0", "t0", "N_t", "ts", "eCO2mean", "eCO2sd"),
              control=list(adapt_delta=0.90,
                           stepsize=0.005),
              chains=4, iter=1000, seed=1234);
```

Here the model is in the same directory as the R markdown knitr doc, but you
could have it anywhere and use a relative path.  The cache.extra command says to
use the contents of the file to determine whether to rerun the block.

At the very top of the document, I just gave everything make-like behavior
with this caching config:

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache=TRUE)
```

which is a game changer in actually updating one of these docs that
happens to have a Stan program that takes 10 minutes to run.

I'll be breaking out my R code, too, once I figure out how to do it.
I really dislike having text and R code and Stan code jumbled into
a single long scrolling doc.  Call me "illiterate."  Just to be clear, I do
believe function specifications (i.e., API doc) and code comments should go
in the code.  Everything else just gets in the way when coding.

Speaking of doc, the best I've found for knitr + R markdown is this:

  http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com

The knitr doc itself, or least what I could find of it, left me very
confused.  I think (but am still not 100% sure), that there are two different
and mostly incompatible ways of using knitr, one with R markdown and HTML to
produce HTML and one with I'm not sure what and LaTeX to produce LaTeX docs.
Others have told me to just use Sweave for LaTeX output.  I was hoping I could
write once and publish in both HTML and PDF to make it easy for us to do things
like document example models.  It's possible, but not all the R
markdown or HTML passes to LaTeX and vice versa, so I still don't know the rules
for making portable docs.  The output's customizable, but has terrible styles
by default in both LaTeX and HTML (and I didn't see any reasonable HTML styles,
so if I keep using this, it's back to CSS for styling --- at least it generates
HTML [though I haven't looked at the generated HTML to see what I'd need to style]).

There's also a book on knitr by its author, Yihui Xie.  The
kindle version looks well converted judging by the sample (CRC seems
to have gotten their act together), but in addition to being $45, it's
already over a year old.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I prefer having separate files, and use Make or other build tools to build everything. But that's not the only way people use it, especially for quick one-off analyses, so I was just offering some alternatives for those who want everything in a single document.  Especially since knitr and other tools like it are widespread in scientific computing and only growing in usage, I just thought it important to make it as easy as possible to use Stan within them.

With the Stan model in a separate file, the other chunk that's useful to add is one to display the model code:

```{r results='markup',echo=FALSE,comment=""}
cat(paste(readLines("foo.stan"), collapse = "\n"))
```

Here's the best way to keep your R code in a separate file while using knitr: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/

Another option is to work backwards from an R file with comments using the spin function: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/stitch/

Knitr is a general report generating environment. So can mix chunks of R (or other programming languages) with a variety of markup languages (actually any markup language, since it is customizable). Markdown and LaTeX are the most common, but you can also use knitr with html, reStructuredText, asciidoc and others.  A bunch of examples of knitr using different markup languages are here: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/.  So if you really hate writing markdown, you can use knitr with html: https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/003-minimal.Rhtml.   But, I think that writing it in markdown is the way to go to produce html & pdf.  But the key is good templates, and separating content from presentation. In my workflow, I use make and knitr for Rmd -> md, and then pandoc to convert the markdown file to either or both html and pdf. I don't rely on the default pandoc templates, but write my own.  Rstudio and the package rmarkdown seem to use their own version of templates which seem to be based on pandoc templates since that's what its using in the background  http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/developer_document_templates.html.

In any case, I have an open pull request to add a Stan engine to knitr https://github.com/yihui/knitr/pull/903 ,  so maybe future versions of knitr will include a Stan engine.

--
Jeffrey Arnold
University of Washington
Acting Assistant Professor of Political Science
Core Faculty Member of the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences

messages.body_plain:
What we do with discontinuities due to dosing is to is to run the
integrator between dosing events.  I hope somebody else can comment
on issues your system may bring up.  It might help to see more of it,
or maybe what you sent is enough for someone to help out.

We don't yet have a way to control tolerances, but we'll
be adding that.  It's not much implementation, but it's a whole
bunch of testing and doc.

The current integrator is indeed prone to hang,

  http://headmyshoulder.github.io/odeint-v2/doc/boost_numeric_odeint/odeint_in_detail/steppers.html

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dormand–Prince_method

As far as we can tell, what's going on is that the parameters are moving
into spaces where the current integrator requires enough steps to reach
tolerance that it effectively hangs.  We haven't figured out an easy way
to limit the max number of steps and also Michael's warning us that may just
bias the results.

We'll be introducing a stiff integrator, hopefully soon, but we're
pretty backed up on issues and feature requests and I'm not sure how
that one's being prioritized.

- Bob

ESS, and org mode?

I've used the latter for a long time, and I find it powerful and
flexible.  It seems to be able to do most if not all of what the former
can do, and it provides a familiar environment that carries across
tasks.

The only two things I sometimes regret are that org mode is so flexible

> On Nov 30, 2014, at 2:51 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ... with

>
> matrix[2, 2] beta;
> vector[2] y[N];
>
> I'd like to do a vectorized calculation involving this:
>
> beta * head(y, N-1)
>

What do you expect that to give you?  head(y, N-1) is
an array of vectors, and we don't support multiplication
for arrays of vectors.  The error you got

> SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
> no matches for function name="multiply"
>     arg 0 type=matrix
>     arg 1 type=vector[1]

is saying that the second argument to the multiplication,
that is head(y, N-1) is an array of vectors.  Stan doesn't
support multiplying a matrix by an array of vectors.

Would you expect to get an array of vectors out?  The only
way to do that is to allocate the array of vectors and
assign the members.

- Bob
